Chapter Eleven: The Classification of the Method for Lighting Lamps from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the method for lighting lamps; by practicing according to this rite, one causes all celestial beings and sages to rejoice and achieve accomplishment."
It may be made of gold as a cup;
or made of silver;
or made of refined copper.
Alternatively, one may use clay or pottery; from among these five types, select whichever one is preferred by the deity for the method of making a lamp wick.
One may make it from white cotton flowers, or from new cotton cloth, or from the fibers of the *nāgakeśara* tree bark.
Alternatively, one may use a wick made of new, clean cloth, employing various fragrant oils that are pleasing to many;
or one may use various fragrant ghee- oils.
For *śāntika* rites, superior fragrant oils are used.
For the pauṣṭika rite, use medium-grade fragrant oil;
for the ābhicāruka rite, use low-grade fragrant oil.
For the śāntika rite, use oil from various fragrant woods.
Sesame oil is used for pauṣṭika rites;
white mustard seed oil is used for ābhicāruka rites;
and the oil of the *āḍhaka* fruit is used for mantra-queens as well as other female seers (*ṛṣikā*).
Various other fruit oils are used by the lords of mantras;
bitter tree fruit oils are used by the various devas;
and fish fat is used by the spirits, such as Mahākāla and others.
The various animal fats are used by the yakṣas;
the oil of *balāde* chickens and sesame oil are used by the lower classes of gods, namely the four sisters such as Cāmuṇḍā and others;
and in the cold forests, the *vaiśravaṇas* and others use dog meat fat.
"Among all oils, black cow ghee is supreme and is universally applicable to the three families; alternatively, white cow ghee is used for *śāntika*,
yellow cow ghee for *pauṣṭika*,
and black cow ghee for *abhicāruka*, or one may use them according to the specific distinctions of their respective sections."
"Among all medicinal herbs, the oil produced from *puṣkaramūla* is for use in *pauṣṭika* rites;
oils extracted from fragrant substances are for use in *śāntika* rites;
and oils with foul odors are for use in *abhicāruka* rites."

"Examine well for yourself the sequence of lighting the lamp as briefly explained above; even if this has not been stated here, apply it with careful scrutiny. If one possesses lamp oil but does not rely upon the specific *kula* (family/division), one should consecrate it by reciting the mantra of that *kula*:
'This offering of a lamp can dispel obstacles, purify, and remove darkness; I now hold it forth in dedication—out of compassion, please accept it.'"
The mantra is: “Ārūka ya ārūka ya sarvavinyardara pūrte svāhā. Having recited this mantra, one should further recite the mantra of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā).
Furthermore, one should again perform the rite of purification after the mantra has been recited, in order to eliminate all faults, as previously explained.

Chapter Twelve: The Offering of Food (*Bali*) The Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Twelve: The Offering of Food "Next, I shall now explain the method for offering food, so that all celestial beings and sages may be fully delighted and swiftly attain accomplishment."
To summarize the offerings for food: one should use round-rooted and long-rooted fruits;
as for items such as ghee cakes, they must not be [ordinary] ghee cakes;
and various other flavors such as soups and stews.
Alternatively, there are various kinds of gruel and beverages;
these four types of food and drink are common to all families (*kula*).
As for the offering of *mṛdvīkā* (raisins) and *pūraga* fruits, they are universally applicable to the three families.
Alternatively, pomegranate or *tinduka* fruit may also be employed for all three families;
according to their respective order, each is restricted to one family.
A sweet taste is used for *śāntika*.
Sweet and sour flavors are used for pauṣṭika rites;
bitter, pungent, and bland flavors are for abhicāruka rites.
The fruits of the tāla tree, the coconut, the bilva, the nīpa, and other malodorous fruits that are disliked by the masses should not be offered.
"There may be fruits of superior flavor that are abundant in the world and most precious; by offering such fruits, one attains the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*).

There may be various fruits whose flavor is moderately delicious, easy to find in the world, and not excessively expensive; by offering such fruits, one attains the middling accomplishment (*madhyamasiddhi*).

There may be various fruits whose flavor is bitter, pungent, or bland, which are plentiful in the world and of the lowest price; by offering such fruits, one attains the inferior accomplishment (*adhamasiddhi*)."
Furthermore, if one wishes to offer with increased devotion, one should take female-named fruits—
namely, persimmons, apricots, peaches, and so forth— and offer them to the Goddess;
and fruits produced by trees that lack a bitter taste should be offered to the Mantra Queen.
The *śrīphala* fruit is common to all the wrathful deities of the three families;
the *vaṇa* fruit is common for seeking all yakṣas;
the *karpūra* fruit is used for the *śrīpuruṣa*.
The *paryaṅka* tree produces fruit, which is used for *paryeṣaka*.
There are many such other varieties of the aforementioned fruits with various names; one should offer them after observing their respective flavors.

"Whether by the side of a village or in a forest hermitage, in a pure location where there are various grass roots with sweet and delicious flavors, one who takes them and offers them will swiftly attain accomplishment."
The *mṛdvīkā* root is suitable for all uses;
furthermore, there is a wondrously delicious flavor that is also suitable for all offerings—not only for celestial deities, but also for use among humans.
“Those roots growing in the mountains that possess a delicious flavor are offered to the Buddha Family; cooked yam roots are likewise applicable to the Buddha Family.
The roots of *kācilindika*, *ciñcālikā*, *vāyasī*, and *kucī*, as well as other round roots, and those produced in water, are used for the Lotus Family.
All medicinal round roots, flowers with bitter or pungent flavors, and various kinds of raw yams are used for the Vajra Family.”
"If a round root is colored white and fragrant with an extremely sweet and full flavor, it is to be offered to the Buddha Family;
if it is yellow in color, possesses moderate fragrance and moderate flavor, being neither too sour nor too sweet, such a round root is for use in the Lotus Family;
if it is red in color, bitter, pungent, or bland in taste, and malodorous or unpleasant, such a round root is for use in the Vajra Family."
In this way, the śāntika and other rites of the three families—superior, middling, and inferior—are all universally applicable.

To summarize: one should offer the complete roots in accordance with the superior, middling, and inferior categories of their respective families; by thus distinguishing them individually, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

As previously stated regarding round roots, long roots, and their growth and uses—such as the varieties of round roots, scallions, garlic, leeks, and other extremely foul-smelling, pungent, or bitter-tasting substances—one should not offer them.
"Śaṣṭika-rice, urubika-rice, pūpa-cakes, vaṇaka and other flour-based foods,
or various kinds of sesame balls; furthermore, various foods made with white sugar,
modakas, maṇḍuṣikas, piṇḍakas, pinḍanikuśika foods, and aśukāvañcikas."
Also *yāsa* food, *śālīya* food, *pūpa* food, *parpaṭaka* food, *śaṣkulīya* food, *pappaṭa* food, *pūpa* food,
*maṇḍapūpa* food, *vinaddhaka* food, *puṣpavarta* food, and *lavaṇika* food.
The food of Ṭakkara, the food of Kumbhāṇḍa, the food of Rākṣasa,
the food of Piśāca, the food of Siddha, the food of Pretakṣudrika,
the food of Śrīpūraka, the food of Vaiśravaṇa, the food of Cchinnaka, and the food of Ṭanaraka.
One encounters the food of *nāṃbulaka*, the food of *citrapuṣpa*, the food of *khyodroḷa*,
the food of *khyonabpatthaśiṅgakaṭa*, the food of *kheta*, various kinds of *ṇavici-bhiṇṇapuṣpa*,
the food of *rāyahaṃsa*, the food of *saryaka*, and the *kṛtampuṣpa*.
Rāga food, kāmuka food, kuśalika food, tripuṭa food, śaṇava food,
harīnaka food, śikhukaṇa food, miṇḍha food, various *pranibhṛtaka* foods, dīpika food, and jala [food].
The food of the *hasitiniyanas*, the food of the *karkaraṇḍakas*,
the food of the *varagatās*, the food of the *vātimṛgas*, the food of the *kṣiptikas*,
the food of the *kāryakarṇikas*, and so forth.
Such foods as these may be prepared using granulated sugar,
or clarified butter,
or sesame seeds mixed together.
As before, one should take and offer whatever belongs to their respective family; by offering according to the ritual, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
"Rice flour and similar foods are for the Buddha Family’s *śāntika* and superior accomplishments;
all wheat-based foods are for the Lotus Family’s *pauṣṭika* and middling accomplishments."
Food prepared with sesame and beans is for the *abhicāruka* rites and lower accomplishments of the Vajra Family.
Among all flavors, that which is adorned with white sugar is for the offering to the Buddha Family; this should always be presented therein.
The *śrīvatsaka* food is used for the Lotus Family.
The *modaka* (joyous ball) is for use in the Vajra Family;
the *pūpa* (cake) is for use in seeking yakṣas;
and the "Woman-named Food" is for use with the Mantra Consorts.
As for the names of the female deities who consume [the offerings]: they are Kāmavajrī, Pāpamitrī, and so forth.
"Among all foods, those that are most precious and delicious should be offered when seeking supreme accomplishment."

Following the sequence of flavors in the other two families, the functions of the eight classes of offerings and so forth are not fully detailed here; rather, they are applied according to their respective roles.

At the time of making the food offering, first spread out cloths, leaves, and the like. For the sake of adornment, first place the *sāṣṭika*, *ulopika*, and *pūpa* offerings. In this manner, one first performs the common rites for the three families.

Furthermore, one should offer whatever food and drink are required for the specific mandala-family according to one's capacity: rice, sixty-day-matured rice, barley milk-porridge, uncultivated self-growing rice, and millet. Whatever is to be offered should be presented according to the ritual rules, along with various fragrant and exquisitely delicious soups, stews, and bean broths, all of which should be respectfully presented.
“Milk-boiled barley rice and non-planted, self-grown *śāli* rice are for seeking the supreme accomplishment;
*śāli* rice and its cooked forms, as well as sixty-day matured *śāli* rice, are for seeking the middling accomplishment;
millet rice and similar grains are for the lower accomplishment.”
"The śāntika rite is for the highest accomplishment;
the pauṣṭika rite is for the middling accomplishment;
and the ābhicāruka rite is for the lowest accomplishment."
"Offerings of cooked food, roots, fruits, rice, and gruel should be presented according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior.
The *śāntika* rite belongs to the supreme Buddha Family;
the *pauṣṭika* rite belongs to the middling Lotus Family."
The *ābhicāruka* rites belong to the Vajra Family.
Regarding the supreme, middling, and inferior *siddhis*, one must skillfully understand their application according to the specific category in accordance with the ritual rules:
"Among soups and broths, those that are sweet and delicious are to be used for *śāntika*."
That which is sour and sweet is used for pauṣṭika;
that which is bitter, pungent, or bland is used for abhicāruka.
"Milk porridge is used for śāntika."
Pomegranate congee, curd congee, and the like are for use in pauṣṭika rites;
kṛsara congee—meaning sesame, non-glutinous rice, beans, and so forth—is for use in ābhicāruka rites.

"As previously explained in brief regarding the various flavors of food and so forth—whether they differ according to region—one should offer them while contemplating their superior, middling, or inferior qualities;
or one should offer those flavors praised by the multitude, or those personally favored, to the Buddha;
or one should follow the sequence for offering food as taught in the mantras of one’s own specific family (*kula*). If one acts otherwise than that, success shall not be attained."
"Among foods, those that are prominent and those with foul odors are used within the Vajra Family.

Regarding the previously mentioned unguents, incense, lamps, food, and so forth, one should first rely on the respective family; furthermore, for rites such as *śāntika*, one should likewise rely on them while observing whether the nature of the mantra is joyful or wrathful."
Next, one should further contemplate what can be accomplished by this;
then, examining it closely, one should consider which aspirations will be fulfilled.
Having observed and understood this, one should offer the previously prepared food according to one's capacity.

Regarding those who see the use of *kāmika* food within the ritual of offerings, one should instead offer *sāṣṭika*, *urubika*, and whatever other food one is able to provide, such as granulated sugar, curd-rice, roots, fruits, milk-porridge, and so forth.
This *kṛmika* food is universally applicable for offerings to all [deities], with the sole exception of *abhicāruka* rites.

If one observes the use of *ciñcā-odana* (sour gruel) within the ritual methods of offering, it should be prepared by adding two or three kinds of superior, extraordinary foods to this *kṛmika* food; this is precisely what is required.
"If one observes that the *ucchuṣma* food is used within the ritual of offerings, it is simply a matter of placing twice as much of the previously mentioned *kāmika* food."
"In the ritual of offering, if one sees the use of the 'three white foods,' these should be understood as milk, curd, and rice with ghee.
Furthermore, if one sees the 'three sweet foods,' these are ghee, honey, and milk-rice."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees *sarvabhojya* food, *sāyallika* food, *laṅgulika* food, *campakapuṣpa* food, *tilapiṣṭaka* food, curd-rice, roots, or fruits—or if one takes any one or two flavors from among the foods previously mentioned and places them there—then one should fill a large vessel with rice-fragrance flowers, various flowers, and leaves, place it in the midst of water, and discard it at a distance from the place of recitation; this is precisely what is meant."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees the *śāntika* food, using *svastika*, milk porridge, rice flour mixed with flowers, ghee, honey, milk, and barley gruel boiled in milk, as well as *vija-pura*, one will certainly be able to eliminate calamities; do not harbor any doubts."

"If one sees the *puṣṭika* [nourishing] food among the offerings, one should employ curd-rice (*yavāgū*), *modaka* cakes, *ulūpikā* sugar-cakes, *śrīvaiṣṭaka*, and other such foods; one will certainly fulfill one's wishes, of this there is no doubt."
"In the ritual of offering, if there is an *abhicāruka* (subjugation) feast, one should use red non-glutinous rice;
or use *kunduruva* seeds;
or use rice dyed red."
Alternatively, by means of sesame cakes, *sāmbhogaka*, *campakapuṣpa*, or *kṣāra-gruel* and the like, one will certainly be able to subdue enemies; of this there is no doubt.

"If one maintains the mantra of a yakṣa but lacks the method for offering food, one should present it according to this rite, using red non-glutinous rice, roots and fruits, honey-water, honey with granulated sugar, rice flour cakes, and so forth."

For the mantras of the female deities (*strī-devatā*) and others, one should offer rice porridge with beans and broth, various sweet drinks and syrups, *prāṇa*, *pṛṣṭaka*, leaf-juices, and so forth, as well as various fruits; all female deities should be offered these foods.

"Those who seek supreme accomplishment and perform the ritual offering should offer according to this: various foods and drinks, roots, fruits, incense, and so forth—abundant, delicious, and highly esteemed by all. These superior flavors are offered while seeking supreme accomplishment."

"The methods for offering food as briefly explained above, along with the specific rites for the goals sought by each respective family (*kula*), have all been set forth in summary. Should there be differences in the flavors of food or drink in other regions, one should observe their colors and tastes and offer them accordingly to the appropriate category."

"When about to present the food, first cleanse and smear the ground, sprinkle it everywhere with scented water, and thoroughly wash the leaves—lotus leaves, *pāṭala* leaves, leaves of various milky trees, or new cotton cloths—and spread them upon it; thereafter, serve the various delicacies using these leaves."
For *śāntika*, one should use the leaves of aquatic plants, other extraordinary trees, or plantain leaves;
for *pauṣṭika*, use the leaves of the *balāka* tree, the *argha* tree, or the *kṛta* tree, or whatever is available at the time;
for *abhicāruka*, use the leaves of female trees, namely:
For the mantras of the female seers (*ṛṣikā*), one should use *bhallātaka* leaves;
for the tree-dwelling deities (*vṛkṣavāsī*), one should use dried tree leaves;
and for the earth-dwelling deities (*bhūmivāsī*), one should use grass.

"One who seeks the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas must know well the proper procedure: first smear and sprinkle the ground, then spread out the leaves; having washed the hands clean and rinsed the mouth several times, one must swallow water before finally partaking of the food."
First, offer the *sāstika* grain;
next, offer round roots, long roots, and fruits;
and further, offer various porridges.
Next, place the various foods below;
next, place the soup and rice below;
next, place the milk and curd below.
Each should descend according to their respective dharmas.

If one constructs a maṇḍala or intends to accomplish various feats and has attained the various states of realization, one should double the offerings of pure food, drink, flowers, fruits, and the like.
"When first performing the recitation, one should offer whatever has been prepared and whatever flavor has been obtained, according to that specific root ritual (*mūla-dharma*).
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, as well as during solar and lunar eclipses or earthquakes, one should perform extensive offerings."

"Prior to the homa, all necessary materials must be prepared and placed before the Honzon; likewise, when the practitioner eats, one portion of food should first be set aside and placed before the Honzon."
If one intends to perform *homa* first and then eat, one should prepare the food in advance and set it out, making offerings beforehand.

Once the food has been prepared, one should then commence the recitation (*japa*), offering various flowers, fruits, and edibles; one must constantly maintain this mindfulness without neglecting it, remaining strictly according to the original ritual manual.
"If one wishes to perform recitation at one time, one should offer roots, fruits, and food as offerings at that same time;
if one wishes to perform recitation at two times, one should offer them at those two times;
if one says one will perform recitation at three times, one should offer them at those three times. By following the ritual in this manner, one shall swiftly achieve accomplishment."

"If a practitioner of recitation does not offer food and drink and violates the rules of their own *kula*, that person will be beset by demonic obstacles; their body will lack vital radiance, they will be afflicted by wind-disorders, cold, hunger, and thirst, and their thoughts will be constantly malevolent. They will be unable to achieve the mantras of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), all because they fail to offer fruit and food to the deity."
One should extensively arrange offerings on the first and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, and present them to the principal deity and their retinue.

When first beginning the recitation, one should prepare *balya* (offering cakes) on such days as those mentioned above and cast them away in the four directions at a distance from the place of recitation.

In this regard, it is not mentioned; or, even if it were permitted within its own class, one should not seek higher accomplishment through inferior flavors, nor should any types of prepared food that are foul-smelling or offensive be used.

One should constantly offer milk-rice; among all the classes [of mantras], those seeking the superior, middling, or inferior *śāntika* rites, as well as those who seek the mantras that universally penetrate the deities, should perform worship in this manner.
If there is no food prepared as originally prescribed, one should recite the mantra of the respective family over whatever has been obtained, saying:
"This medicine is of rare fragrance and exquisite flavor; it is fit only for offering to the Honored One!"
"I now offer this to you; please accept it out of compassion.
"A-ha-ra | A-ha-ra | Sarva-vibhīta-dara-pūrdhe | Svāhā. After this mantra has been universally applied to all three families, one should recite and maintain the mantra of the specific deity.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on the Śāntika Rite.

Regarding the Śāntika rite, the Pauṣṭika rite, and the Ābhicāruka rite, although they were previously explained in general terms, they have not yet been fully detailed; therefore, I shall now once again proclaim them to extensively clarify their principles.
Regarding these three types of rites that are swiftly accomplished, one should practice them in their proper sequence according to the Dharma.

"If one performs the *śāntika* recitation and the *homa* rite for averting calamities, one should take refuge in the Triple Gem and give rise to a profound mind of compassion; beginning at dusk on the first day of the waxing moon, one should commence the recitation and uphold the *śāntika* rite."
At this time, the Śuddhāvāsa deities descend from heaven to wander among humans; through their celestial blessings, one will swiftly attain siddhi.
Clad in white garments and seated upon kuśa grass, facing north with body and mind in tranquil stillness, one performs the śāntika rite.
First, take cow dung that has not yet fallen to the ground and smear it on the ground three times, scattering white flowers everywhere.

If one performs *homa*, first prepare barley, milk curds, rice grains, sesame seeds, *śyāmāka* grain, *darbha* grass, *pāṭalā* flowers, and boiled non-glutinous rice; then use dried white flowers and dried flower stamens, employing *śamī* wood, or various resinous incense woods, or *naktamālaka* wood.
Alternatively, one may use various milky trees; one should take the tips of their branches, not discarding the leaves, and cut them to the proper length.
Or one may use ghee and honey.

These materials for *homa* are universally applicable across all families (*kula*). If there are specific instructions mentioned in the primary ritual manual (*mūla-vidhi*), one should follow those to perform the *śāntika* rite.
Take nine pieces from a milky tree by rubbing them together, or take them from a suitable location and perform the *homa* offering; by performing the *śāntika* rite, success will be swiftly attained.

Cut a branch of a milky tree to the length of one span (*vitasti*), and mix it with ghee, honey, milk, and other substances within a vessel. Kindle a fire using dry wood from a milky tree and perform the *homa*, or, at a pure place such as a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), kindle a superior fire using dry cow dung;
or use *śamī* wood.
Alternatively, for a *śāntika* rite, one may use various fragrant woods.

The firewood should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length, and the hearth should be made in the shape of a ball. The ground must be a clean, white area; it should be dug to a depth of twelve finger-widths, measured by the span of the thumb.
The rafters above the *kāṅ* (ridge-pole) shall all measure four finger-widths; within the *kāṅ*, a wheel shall be made measuring four inches, with a height of one finger-width.

The practitioner, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), should focus upon the object of practice according to the ritual of their respective *kula*. Just as one performs offerings based on the ritual of making offerings to the Buddhas' compassion, one should likewise [invoke] the Tathāgata-vajra-locanā, the Vidyārājñī, Prajñāpāramitā, and Buddhalocanā;
next, one makes offerings to the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
Next, offer to the Śuddhāvāsa devas; next, to the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, and so forth.

With the Lord of the Root Mantra seated in the center, the Buddha sits to his left. Next are seated the Bodhisattvas: Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Ākāśagarbha, Kṣitigarbha, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and others. Following them are the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and so on, down to the nāga king Nanda at the western gate. To his right are the Tathāgata’s Ūrṇā Prajñā, the Mahā-ustnīṣa-sitātapatra, the Sitātapatra, and the Tejorāśi-uṣṇīṣa.

Chapter 14: The Ritual for Pauṣṭika, from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. Regarding the ritual for *pauṣṭika*: with a heart full of joy, one should perform recitation, retention, or *homā* according to the specific family (*kula*) to which one belongs. One should begin on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon and conclude on the fifteenth day of the subsequent waxing moon, performing the *pauṣṭika* rites while remaining within that particular family.
Furthermore, beginning from the hour of the Tiger (3–5 a.m. and continuing until midday, one should act entirely in accordance with one's original intention.

When beginning at this time, the various assemblies of noble devas are wandering and observing the world; moreover, Śakra and other celestial beings, as well as the various Dharma-devas, descend at that moment to inspect the world. Seeing those who promote goodness, they feel joy in their hearts and are able to fulfill their aspirations.

"When the practitioner reaches this stage, they should be sincere and not indolent; wearing white garments and facing east, they should sit in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture to perform the *puṣṭika* rite. They should smear the ground with various fine incenses at the three periods of the day and scatter flowers of various colors everywhere upon that ground."
If one performs a homa, it should be conducted according to this: using thick milk-rice porridge, or ghee, milk, and honey;
or a mixture of four substances consisting of ghee, honey, curd, and sesame seeds;
or simply using ghee alone.
Alternatively, one may use empty curd; or madanapuspa; or bilva fruit.
Alternatively, one may use non-glutinous rice;
or the juice of the *nāgakesara* flower;
or a lotus flower.
Alternatively, one may use *kṛṣṇa* flowers, taking one from each variety and performing *homa* by dipping them in clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Or one may use curd-rice;
or take any of the various seeds; or use branches from milky trees and other such items as previously described, performing the *puṣṭika* rite according to the original ritual manual.
"Take fire from a Kṣatriya household, or produce fire by rubbing together pieces of wood from the royal palace;
or take a great fire—whosoever obtains such fire shall find it entirely auspicious."

Take a handful of wood, one cubit in length, and perform homa by anointing it with ghee, milk, and curd. First, kindle a fire using wood from a milky tree, or use wood from flowering or fruit-bearing trees as fuel for the fire on black earth.

If such a site is unavailable, one should take black earth from an external location to fill a trench, and upon it construct a hearth two cubits square and one cubit deep. Within the trench, fashion a lotus flower measuring two finger-widths across and four finger-widths in height; the rafters should be one span wide.

Both the interior and exterior should be smeared with black earth, and it should be constructed according to the ritual of its respective family. One must contemplate the original causal conditions clearly and without interruption or forgetfulness.
"In the *pauṣṭika* [rite], one should place Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in front;
Mahāsthāmaprāpta on the right side; and on this left side, place the Vidyārāja of Avalokiteśvara and others;
on the right side, Siddhārtha the Vidyārāja and the ṛṣis; and on this left side, place the bodhisattvas."
In this place, one should further install the deities such as the Seven Auspicious Ones;
next, the Vidyārāja;
and next, Brahmā surrounded by his host of Brahmā-devas. For the sake of seeking one's aspirations, one may also at will offer worship to yakṣas and the maharṣi Ārdraka.
Even among the various celestial and divine assemblies within the Padma family, each performs according to the Dharma:
first performing self-consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and then reciting mantras to perform *puṣṭika* rites, seeking long life;
or seeking the regrowth of fallen teeth, and the turning of white hair back to black.
Whether seeking the nourishment and vigor of the limbs, the increase of merit and power,
or various other virtues— whatever one desires in the mind and makes such a vow is called *puṣṭika*.

Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on Abhicāruka From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on Abhicāruka. Regarding *abhicāruka*: one harbors anger in the heart; being angry with the object of the rite, one is oneself free from fear.
One should perform this rite by reciting the wrathful mantra, or by performing homa; one need not select specific days or times, nor observe fasting vows.
One should begin during a time of wrath. If one observes the calendar, it is on the eighth or fifteenth day of the dark fortnight at midday;

or at a time when the *piśācas*, *bhūtas*, *rākṣasas*, and other such hosts have gathered together or are roaming through a particular location. Performing the *abhicāruka* rite at such a time, with a mind of wrath, makes accomplishment easy to attain.
The various other classes of spirits will assist the practitioner of recitation, causing their wrath to increase and ensuring that the task at hand is swiftly accomplished.

Wearing red or blue garments, one should moisten them with water before putting them on; for extremely wrathful rites, one should moisten them with one's own blood. Standing with the right foot treading upon the left, facing south, with eyes wide open and uneven, brows furrowed in anger between the eyebrows, gnashing the teeth and making a great sound, one should visualize oneself as the Lord of this family, enduring physical and mental exhaustion with fortitude.
If one performs an ābhicāruka rite according to this sequence of dharmas, one should take black earth at three times each day to smear upon the maṇḍala, or use donkey dung;
or the dung of sheep, pigs, or dogs; or the ashes of a cremated corpse; and offer flowers of red fragrance, or flowers that have a foul odor.
Or [offerings] that are blue;
or one may offer the husks of various grains, wheat, and beans.
At the time of the homa, white mustard seeds are used.
Either mustard oil;
or one's own blood;
or again, using salt;
Alternatively, one may use mustard seeds;
or the leaves of the bitter *kṣāra* plant;
or again, one may use ashes.
Or using dust from the soles of the feet;
or using donkey dung;
or the dung of camels, dogs, pigs, sheep, or human excrement, and so forth.
Alternatively, one may use hair or body fur, pounded into a paste; or use a crow;
or use a hawk, a vulture, a crane, a magpie, or other such birds.
Alternatively, one may use its bile;
or use feathers and down;
or use the fats of the aforementioned birds and beasts, and so forth.
Or using thorns;
or broken pottery shards;
or various scattered bones;
Or using dog meat;
or pork and so forth;
or *kvathana* wood;
Some are wood used for the practice of ascetic mortification;
some are wood used for cremating corpses;
some are the remains of wood used for cremating corpses; and some are thorny wood.
Alternatively, one may use khadira wood, cutting it according to the ritual rules for use in homa.
Whichever of these types of materials is employed, each should be mixed with three substances: poison, one's own blood, and salt.
Alternatively, for whatever rite is to be performed, one should take fire from a cremation pyre or from the house of a *caṇḍāla*;
or else, one may produce fire by striking bone with a stone.
From the tree previously mentioned, one should take a piece measuring ten finger-widths from its root, split both ends so that they are pointed, and smear it with poison and mustard oil.
When setting fire to it, use dry, pungent, and malodorous wood, or wood from a corpse-bearing tree;

alternatively, first ignite wood remaining from a cremation. In black soil, dig a triangular hearth with one corner facing outward. Each side of the triangle should be twenty finger-widths long, ten finger-widths deep, and three finger-widths wide at the top; then smear it with the ashes of a cremated corpse.
The base of the hearth should be measured by the span of a human hand; the *vajra* [stūpa] should be three finger-widths high, made from the ashes of cremated corpses,
or using various husks, or using charcoal,
or taking substances for *homa*, namely:
Using poisons, various excrement, mustard seeds, salt, and so forth,
one should fashion the form of that enemy and perform homa by cutting that form into pieces;
or, one may place one’s left foot upon the heart of the form while performing homa.
As it is with the homa, so it is with the recitation; one may either cut the branches with a knife,
or lash them with a staff,
or pierce them with the thorns of the soapberry tree.
Alternatively, one may strike it with a staff made of khadira wood.

This applies universally across all sections, and the ritual procedures are as previously stated; one should rely upon and employ the primary method as it is proclaimed. As extensively explained before, one must not forget the mental focus regarding the circumstances of the rites performed through the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the ritual rules.
"When performing this rite, first make offerings to the Great Wrathful Vajra (Mahākrodhavajra) and all his retinue;
offer them all. First, place the Vidyārājñī Vajrāṅkuśī;
next, place the Vidyārāja Kuliśamuṣṭi, which in this language means 'Vajra-Eater'."
Next is Mahāmāri, here translated as the Great Death Vidyārāja;
next is Śatākṣī, here translated as the Six-Hundred-Eyed Vidyārāja;
followed by the nāgas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and so forth.

"One should first protect oneself by applying the *śāntika* mantra; then, having prepared the offerings according to the ritual, one performs the *abhicāruka* rite to cause the limbs of the enemies to become separated, or to move them from their original locations,
or to cause those who are close to hate one another,
or to afflict them with severe illness."
Or they may cause their kinsmen to be scattered;
or they may render them stubborn and foolish;
or they may commit various other evil deeds.
Performing such rites is termed *abhicāruka*.

One who commits these evil acts does so to punish evildoers who harbor ill will toward the Triple Gem or seek its faults, desiring that they may experience slight suffering in the present life to avoid the calamities of hell.
Seeing sentient beings committing various kinds of transgressions— whether they violate the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva,
slander the Triple Gem,
or act in opposition toward their teachers— one performs the ābhicāruka rite out of compassion for them.
"When performing this rite, one must rely upon one's own specific family (kula);
one must not arbitrarily employ wrathful mantras, or the mantras of various malevolent rākṣasas,
or the mantras of the *pāliśi* messengers to perform this *abhicāruka*."
Having performed this rite to punish the wicked and fulfill one's wishes, one should gaze at them with eyes full of wrath and apply further measures.

For those who are gravely ill or whose death is imminent, one should quickly perform a *śāntika* rite; thereafter, one may slowly perform a *pauṣṭika* rite. This [aggressive] method should not be employed in such cases.

When performing this rite, it is best to employ the mantras of the Rākṣasas or follow the specific ritual manual (*dharmapāṭha*); even if using a mantra from the Buddha Family, there is no cause for fear.

When applying this method to punish an evil person, one must be free from resentment and possess great compassion, considering that the person’s evil karma will cause them to suffer for a long time. Since their constant practice of evil only prolongs the causes of suffering, you should perform this rite out of a desire to grant them eternal peace and happiness; however, you must not harbor a mind of anger.
Those who commit evil deeds ought to fall into hell; however, because the Lords of Mantras wish to remove the sufferings of hell, they employ such skillful means to rescue and protect them.

One should observe whether the karmic actions of those evildoers are light or heavy and apply the corresponding remedy accordingly. One must not cause death for a minor offense, nor should one inflict excessive pain upon others for the sake of treating that [offender]. Rather, in order to bring them joy, one should perform the *śāntika* rite.

"At that time, whether using that same hearth or preparing another one, perform the *śāntika* rite by means of *homa* with milk. By removing the names such as 'hana hana, paca paca, māra māra' from the *abhicāruka* mantra and substituting the name 'śāntikuru,' the *śāntika* rite is accomplished."

"Since you have already turned your minds [toward awakening], you should contemplate bodhicitta and give rise to the mind of enlightenment; you should always harbor thoughts of benefiting all sentient beings. How could it be appropriate for you to practice such a dharma?"

One should perform the *abhicāruka* rite by the side of a pond;

Chapter Sixteen: The Classification of Methods for Accomplishment (*Siddhi-vibhāga-paṭala*) from the Susiddhikara Sūtra, also titled "The Chapter on the Signs of Siddhi. Furthermore, regarding the attainment of *siddhi*, advancing through the air is the most supreme.
Concealing one's form and hiding one's traces constitutes middling accomplishment;
worldly affairs constitute the lower *siddhi*.

There are these three types—superior, middling, and inferior—namely, the three kinds of accomplishment consisting of traveling through the air, invisibility, and worldly matters, which are further distinguished according to their superior, middling, and inferior degrees.
"The three families are fully accomplished; I shall now expound them once more.
The Vidyādharas achieve the five supernormal powers by traveling through the air, and there are many varieties:
some attain the exhaustion of all outflows."
Some are pratyekabuddhas;
some have realized the stages and grounds of bodhisattvas;
and some understand and comprehend all phenomena.
Some possess eloquence and extensive learning;
some achieve the *vaitālīya* meter;
and some achieve the state of a yakṣiṇī.
Or one may obtain a cintāmaṇi jewel;
or one may obtain an inexhaustible hidden treasure.
Possessing such matters as these constitutes the supreme-superior accomplishment (*uttamottama-siddhi*).
"Next, within the three families, the methods for middling accomplishment are explained: becoming invisible and concealing one's traces;
the body attaining great power;
and transforming prior indolence into diligent application."
Entering the palace of the asuras, one obtains the medicine of longevity;
one becomes a *pāriṣadya* heavenly messenger;
or one is able to command spirits.
Some may achieve mastery over the tree deity Śarabhaṇḍika;
some may become widely learned, such that even regarding what they have not yet heard, they deeply understand its meaning and principles;
or they may succeed in compounding medicines, so that by merely applying them to their feet or heads, they can travel vast distances without experiencing any fatigue.
The siddhis described above are called middling-superior accomplishments (*madhyottama-siddhi*).
Next, the methods for inferior-middling accomplishments (*hīnamadhyama-siddhi*) are explained:
by the power of mantras, one causes all beings to behold one with joy.
Either to subdue the masses;
or to be able to punish evildoers, subdue various enemies, and attend to other lesser matters—
these constitute the superior, middling, and inferior [levels].
"If one wishes to accomplish the medicinal *yoga* and so forth, there are three grades of accomplishment:
the arising of light and flames is superior; the appearance of smoke is middling; and warmth is inferior."
"Furthermore, the mantras of the Noble Ones (ārya) constitute the supreme accomplishment;
those spoken by the gods (deva) are called the middling accomplishment;
and the mantras of worldly beings (laukika) are the inferior accomplishment."
"Furthermore, the mantras of the Buddha Family result in the superior siddhi;
the mantras of the Lotus Family result in the middling siddhi;
and the Vajra Family results in the inferior siddhi."
"If one desires to seek the lower [attainment] by means of a superior mantra, one will obtain the lower accomplishment;
or if one desires to seek the superior [attainment] by means of an inferior mantra, one will obtain the superior accomplishment;
or if one employs a middling mantra to accomplish either the higher or the lower, it is likewise equal."
"Within the mantra these four virtues are contained; one should know that the superior, middling, and inferior divisions of the mantra can bring about great fruits and rewards, namely:
fulfilling the stage of a Pratyekabuddha;
and fulfilling the ten stages of a Bodhisattva."
It culminates in the great fruit of attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, it accomplishes great virtuous conduct, namely:
being surrounded by a vast retinue of followers before and behind; for one who fulfills such a vow, this constitutes great virtuous conduct.

Furthermore, there is the stage of long-term abiding, which refers to those who have attained the state of a superior station or a wheel-turning station as long-lived seers; those who fulfill such vows are said to abide for a long time.
Furthermore, its form and appearance are vast and great,
meaning that its majestic radiance shines afar constitutes its vastness of form.
One who possesses these four virtues can achieve the superior grade even with a mantra of the inferior grade.
Among those of the superior grade, if one does not possess these virtues, although they may be a practitioner of superior mantras, their application is that of the inferior grade.

Regarding the mantras spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, according to this successive order, even those spoken by many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can accomplish matters of the superior grade and so forth, despite being classified as belonging to the inferior grade.
"Among the mantras taught by the Honored Ones and others, some possess only a single function;
namely, the śāntika rite, the pauṣṭika rite, and the ābhicāruka rite."
Although each possesses one of these factors, within them there are respectively superior, middling, and inferior grades. How could an inferior-grade mantra accomplish a superior task?
It is certainly no doubt that a wondrous lotus flower emerges from blue mud;
yet how could a superior-grade mantra of benevolence and compassion accomplish an inferior-grade accomplishment of wrath?
Just as white sandalwood is cooling by nature, yet fire naturally arises when it is struck by the wind or rubbed together, this is not without causes and conditions.
Likewise, although these various differences do not follow a fixed sequence, you should have no doubts regarding any of the other *siddhis*.
“Siddhi of the body is the superior accomplishment;
siddhi of medicinal herbs is the middling accomplishment;
and siddhi of abundance is the inferior accomplishment.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who has long been reciting an inferior-grade mantra, even if they personally lack the power to seek a superior-grade one from the deity, the deity will graciously bestow it upon them.

However, if regarding a superior-grade mantra they harbor doubts, or if their recitation and offerings are not sincere, then although it is a superior-grade mantra, because their mind during recitation is light, they will only attract an inferior-grade accomplishment.

Therefore, know that the practice of recitation depends entirely upon the mind and intention. For instance, among the gods there are those who are poor, and within the ranks of the spirits there are those who are wealthy and powerful; as it is with these beings, so it is with mantras.
Each and every mantra possesses the three *siddhis*, namely the superior, middling, and inferior; by reciting them with a sincere heart, one shall obtain *siddhi*. Chapter Seventeen:
