When the recitation is finished, one should perform the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*). At the time of dismissal, one should protect oneself by using the mantra of that Lord of the Family, or the mantra of the Lord of the Family, or the Family Mother (*kula-mātṛ*), or the Family Heart (*kula-hṛdaya*), and then proceed as desired.

"If one must go to a defiled place, an impure location, or any such site for some necessary business, one should first recite the mantra of Ucchuṣma and form its mudrā, sealing the five places [of the body] before proceeding as one pleases; furthermore, one must constantly recite that mantra and never allow it to be forgotten."
At the time of bathing, one should first recite the *Vighnāntaka* mantra to protect the body; this should not be neglected from the start until the bath is completed.
The *Vighnāntaka* mantra is that of Kumāra.
At the time of eating, one should use the mantra of the presiding deity of the respective family (*kula*) to protect the body while maintaining mindfulness.
When about to lie down, one should protect the body with the mantra of the Mother of the Family (*kulamātṛ*).

If, while performing various rites, one forgets to perform the protective methods, demons will now arise. To eliminate these demons, one should quickly recite and hold the mantra of the Vidyārāja of that particular family to protect oneself; thus, no demonic obstacles shall find an opportunity.
"Once the aforementioned methods for protecting the body, binding the boundaries, and other rites have been performed, one should then collect the mind and perform the recitation with composure.

Regarding the seat required by the practitioner for recitation: it should be made of blue *kuśa* grass, four finger-widths high, one span wide, and sixteen finger-widths long. Such a seat should be used both at the commencement of the recitation and during its performance."
Alternatively, one may use *kāśa* grass (pronounced with a departing tone); or other green grasses;
or, according to the ritual methods of the respective family (*kula*), one may select a milky tree, as using its wood is most essential and sublime.
One should prepare a seat according to the measurements previously described and thoroughly clear and level the ground;
alternatively, one may use various leaves,
or construct it from branches and stalks as mentioned above, taking branches and leaves for a seat in accordance with the requirements of the practice.
"On that seat, one should sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) to perform śāntika and the superior accomplishments;
in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka) to perform pauṣṭika and the middling accomplishments;
and with both feet hanging down to perform ābhicāruka and the inferior accomplishments."
"When the offerings have been completed, one should arouse a sincere heart to praise the Buddha;
next, praise the Dharma and the Sangha;
and next, Avalokiteśvara."
Next, one praises the Greatly Compassionate King of Great Power Vajra in the same manner:
"Greatly compassionate savior of sentient beings, Skillfully guiding toward all-knowledge;
Ocean of merit and virtue, I now prostrate to the Buddha!"
Able to purify the poisons of greed and hatred, Skillfully eliminating all evil destinies;
The principle of ever-present suchness— I now pay homage to that Dharma!
Having attained those gates of liberation, They dwell well within the various precepts.
To the supreme field of merit and virtue, I now pay homage to that Saṅgha!
Praised by all Buddhas alike, capable of generating manifold blessings,
they are called Avalokiteśvara!
I now prostrate with my head in homage to the body of great power and wrath!
Excellent, O Lord of Vidyādharas!
"I now prostrate in homage to those who have subdued what is difficult to subdue.

Having thus praised the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with such devotion, he again joined his palms and, arising with a heart of profound reverence, praised the virtues of the Buddhas and other Bodhisattvas.
The text for this praise should employ the eulogies spoken by the assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; one should not compose it oneself.
Once the praise is completed, one should arise with a heart of utmost sincerity and repent for all transgressions, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Arhats, Noble Sangha, and all Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions!"

We acknowledge that from the past until this present life, our minds have been shrouded by afflictions as we have long wandered through birth and death; and in other lives, we have committed various evil karmas while obscured by greed, hatred, and delusion—whether toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha;
or toward Arhats, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of saints;
or toward our parents, elders, and other sentient beings, whether they possessed virtue or not.

Having committed various evil deeds in the aforementioned places—whether performed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in when seen—and having extensively accumulated all manner of transgressions through the actions of body, speech, and mind, one should join the palms with a sincere heart and prostrate before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Thus, having repeatedly repented for the multitude of offenses committed through unwholesome karma, and having confessed them all according to the Dharma as known by the Buddha, one should give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity and, for the remainder of one's life, take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and in the true path of Nirvāṇa.
‘In order to eliminate the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings, I take refuge in the Triple Gem.
With a mind of profound reverence, one should thus take refuge and prostrate with the head and face at their feet.

Next, one should again give rise to a sincere mind to seek the supreme fruit of liberation, the nectar of immortality; with a heart full of exultation, one should resolve upon bodhicitta and seek the fruit of *siddhi*. [One should think:
"I shall eliminate the immeasurable sufferings of the Dharma for all sentient beings in the world, and further deliver them so that they may leave behind all evil destinies;
I shall cause them to attain liberation from all afflictions."
Seeing all sentient beings tormented by various kinds of suffering, one gives rise to great compassion and awakens the bodhicitta;
one acts as a refuge for those afflicted by suffering;
and for those who have no master, one shall become their master.
He acts as a guide for sentient beings who have lost their way;
he provides fearlessness to sentient beings who are terrified;
and he brings peace and happiness to sentient beings who are suffering and distressed.
Sentient beings are oppressed by various afflictions; I shall eliminate them for their sake.

Whatever other wholesome deeds I have performed and whatever merit has arisen from generating this superior resolve, I dedicate them all to sentient beings so that they may return to the correct path.
Furthermore, the gates of the six *pāramitās* and all other merits I have created, I dedicate to sentient beings so that we may together attain the supreme fruit.

From the past, present, and future, briefly speaking, may all the supreme merit I have created be dedicated to all sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain the Buddha-way up to enlightenment; may I never give rise to indolence but instead arouse the bodhicitta, and with compassionate concern for all sentient beings, give rise to great loving-kindness.
When will their manifold sufferings be extinguished?

For the sake of purifying the mind, they should constantly maintain the six recollections; recollecting these six recollections with one-pointed concentration, they should not allow the mind to scatter nor should they harbor self-clinging.
Furthermore, just as the Buddhas of the past made their vows, one should likewise make this vow: "May all pure karma produced be dedicated to sentient beings so that they may accomplish all virtues;

furthermore, may the merit I produce cause all sentient beings to obtain inexhaustible wealth, and may they further be able to practice giving, increase their wisdom, achieve great patience, constantly cultivate wholesome qualities, always possess knowledge of past lives, and ever cherish great compassion."
"In all the places where various classes of sentient beings are born, they possess the aforementioned conditions.
Next, one should join the palms and prostrate to the Lord of the Family, the Mantra King Smṛtijñānakīrti;

then, according to the ritual rules, perform the various activities. First, take the rosary with the right hand and place it in the left hand; holding it with joined palms, contemplate the Mantra King and recite the mantra for the purpose of using the rosary:
The mantra of the Vajra Family is:
“Namaḥ ratnatrayāya, namaḥ mañjuśriye vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye, oṃ kili kili lāḍanī svāhā. The mantra of the Buddha Family is:
“Namaḥ ratnatrayāya, oṃ anabhūte vijaye siddharate svāhā. The mantra of the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ amṛtadharme śrīye śrīmālini svāhā. Joining the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands, perform the recitation with the right hand; this is effective for all purposes.
If performing an ābhicāruka rite, one should extend the thumb and form the mudrā of counting the rosary beads.
Bodhi seeds are used for recitation in the Buddha Family;
lotus seeds are used for the Avalokiteśvara Family.
The *rudrākṣa* seed is for the Vajra family;
it is used universally across all three families as previously described. These rosaries are the most excellent and supreme; one should hold them during all recitations.
Alternatively, one may use wood from the khadira tree;
or seeds from the tāla tree;
or even fashion them from clay.
Some are made from conch shells;
some from crystal, or from pearls;
or they are made from ivory.
Alternatively, one may use red pearls;
or various maṇi jewels;
or use *yava* seeds and other grass seeds, each according to its respective family (*kula*), observing their color and type to select them for recitation and retention.

If one performs the *ābhicāruka* rite, one should use various bones to fashion a rosary; thus one will swiftly attain accomplishment. Furthermore, for the sake of the efficacy of the *rakṣā*, *śāntika*, and *puṣṭika* rites, one should additionally recite [the mantra].
The mantra of the Buddha Family is:
“Oṃ namo bhagavati siddhe svadhārataye svāhā. The mantra for increasing the efficacy of the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ vasumati śrīye svāhā. The mantra for increasing the efficacy of the Vajra Family is:
"Oṃ vāgīśvari jaḥ svāhā. Recite this while using the aforementioned bead-seal (*mālāmudrā*).
During recitation, place the beads at the heart center; they must not be held too high or too low.
When holding the rosary, one should bow the head slightly and, with a mind of sincere devotion, pay homage to the Triple Gem;
next, pay homage to the eight great bodhisattvas;
and next, pay homage to the vidyārāja and his retinue.

Next, one should begin the recitation of the mantra, visualizing the Lord of Mantras as if standing before one's eyes; thus, with sincere devotion, one must not allow the mind to be distracted by other objects.

"However, regarding those mantras that begin with the syllable 'Oṃ' and the syllables 'Namaḥkāraṇa' and so forth, one should recite them with a tranquil mind; during śāntika rites and pauṣṭika rites, they should all be recited slowly or mentally.
Furthermore, it should be known that for those mantras which end with the syllable 'Hūṃ' or the syllable 'Phaṭ', they should all be recited with a forceful voice."

When performing *abhicāruka* rites or other wrathful activities, one should examine the number of syllables in the mantra. If there are fifteen syllables, one should recite it fifteen lakṣas of times; if there are thirty-three syllables, one should recite it three lakṣas of times; for those exceeding this number, one should recite ten thousand times as described above.
"When reciting for the first time, one completes the aforementioned number [of repetitions]; one examines its categories as superior, middling, or inferior;
or its three types of matters;
or one examines what was spoken by the Noble Ones."

It is taught for the devas—meaning it is taught for the earth-dwelling devas; one should carefully examine the categories [of practitioners] and recite and maintain it until accomplishment is attained.

If one does not first recite it in this manner, but instead merely maintains it through general mindfulness, even the lower rites sought will not be achieved for long, let alone the higher or middling *siddhi* accomplishments.
For this reason, one should first perform recitation with a most exalted mind.

As previously explained regarding the initial recitation and retention of mantras, one should divide the total number of recitations into ten parts; then, once the recitation is complete, one should pray to the Lord of Mantras for the causes and conditions of *siddhi*.
If no signs appear, one should thus pray a second and a third time from the beginning;
if signs do appear, one should then recite the mantra according to the ritual rules;
if no such state arises, one should abandon it and not recite.

"The method for requesting [the deity's presence] is the same as the method for summoning. When making the request, if one sees the Lord of Mantras in a dream turning his back and departing, or not speaking with one, one must begin the recitation anew; this should be done two or three times.
If in a dream one sees the Lord of Mantras conversing, it should be known that this person will achieve accomplishment before long.
If there is no such vision, one should not perform the recitation; if one forces oneself to recite and maintain it, it will bring misfortune upon others."

"When first beginning the recitation, one should commence the practice in a pure and secluded place; from the first day of recitation until exhaustion, the number of repetitions must strictly follow the fixed requirement and should neither be increased nor decreased."
"Regarding the previously mentioned recitation during the three periods:
one should perform the recitation during the first and last parts of the day; during the middle part, one should engage in bathing and performing various virtuous deeds.

At night, there are likewise three periods as above; during the middle part, one should attend to rest and other such matters. Performing the recitation during this [middle] portion of the night for the sake of performing *ābhicāruka* rites, *āntardhāna* rites, and rites for rousing [the deity], is said to be most excellent."
"If one performs recitation by day and homa by night;
or if one maintains recitation during the night and performs homa by day, provided that many medicinal substances are prepared—
performing homa before the recitation and performing homa again after the recitation is finished— if one can do so in this manner, it is the most excellent."

"As previously stated, one should perform homa with the *piṇḍa* food; regardless of whether it precedes or follows other rites, one should always recite the mantra and perform homa according to this method.

Furthermore, if within a rite success is attained by performing only the homa, you should know that it is nonetheless necessary to recite the mantra. If one acts in this manner, the vidyās will be pleased and the signs of efficacy will be easily accomplished."
"The practitioner should not give rise to anger;
should not seek sensual pleasures;
and should not disparage themselves."
Without wearying oneself through toil and hardship;
without giving rise to fear;
and without seeking with excessive diligence.
Do not give rise to contempt or arrogance.

While reciting, do not engage in idle talk; even if the body is utterly exhausted, do not indulge in it. Restrain all evil influences and do not think of worldly conversation. Do not abandon the *iṣṭadevatā*, and even if you see extraordinary signs, you should not regard them with wonder.
Furthermore, while reciting, do not discriminate among various appearances.
When the recitation is completed, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family, or the mantra of the Mother of the Family;
by reciting these mantras, one shall obtain protection such that no obstacles can arise.
"Once you have completed the recitation according to this ritual method—even if you exceed the prescribed number—do not be apprehensive. You should arouse a sincere heart and make this supplication:
'I have completed the full number of recitations according to this ritual method; I pray only that the Venerable One will accept them as proof and grant me instructions within my dreams.'"

"If, while reciting with right mindfulness, one suddenly coughs, yawns, passes gas, or forgets a syllable of the mantra, one should immediately rise and go to water to perform the ritual of *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling purification). Even if one has already counted the beads and is short by only one round, upon encountering such an affliction, once the *prokṣaṇa* is completed, one must begin the recitation again from the beginning."
Regarding the obstacles to the Path mentioned above, one must contemplate each one from the beginning.
When the counting of the prayer beads is nearly finished, perform one prostration; when it is completed and one begins again, perform another prostration.

Before the scroll, or at the place of the image, or before the stūpa, or at the seat, wherever one recites the mantra, one should perform one circumambulation with the rosary, gaze upon the countenance of the Honored One once, and prostrate once.
Having completed the recitation as previously described, settle the mind in a quiet place and visualize the mantra and its presiding deity.

Regarding the three times of recitation—morning, noon, and evening—one must apply the mind with sincere devotion; the number of repetitions must remain consistent across all sessions, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Furthermore, bathing, smearing the ground, offering flowers, removing withered blossoms, and all such various acts of worship must be performed at each of the three times.

"One should possess the three robes; furthermore, one should wash the inner robe at the three times of day to cleanse the body. When it is dry, one is permitted to fumigate it with incense or sprinkle it with purified water; during each of these periods, one may perform whichever of these practices is appropriate."

Set aside separate garments for sleeping and bathing; change these undergarments at these two times and wash them once every day. If these clothes are difficult to clean, allow them to be fumigated and sun-dried.
One should wash the offering vessels and bowls three times a day; once the withered flowers have been removed, one should replace them with fresh ones;
and at the three times of the day, one should constantly recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and perform the rites of the caitya and the maṇḍala.

First, one should recite the mantra of service; once this is completed, if one has not yet obtained the requested boon, one must not allow it to be neglected or interrupted. One should continue the recitation at one, two, or even three sessions a day, without any break.

"If one is possessed by demonic obstacles, afflicted by the karma of illness, lacks sincerity of mind and is constantly negligent, suffers physical and mental exhaustion, disregards the proper seasons, or fails to act according to the rules—such as failing to bathe at the appropriate times—then the recitations and homas performed in such a manner should not be counted.
Only those who practice with a concentrated mind, acting in accordance with the Dharma and maintaining the mantra, and who possess these qualities, should have their counts recorded."

"Regarding the three matters of performing homa, reciting mantras, and invoking deities, the total number of mantra recitations for each will not be accomplished unless they are all fulfilled according to the prescribed rules. Even if the count is nearly complete, lacking only one repetition, if an obstacle arises, one must begin counting from the beginning once more."

"If one constructs a maṇḍala according to the ritual, or performs recitation at these two times—during solar or lunar eclipses—the merit will increase and there is no doubt that accomplishment will be attained before long;
or at the eight great sacred stūpas, or at places where past Buddhas practiced their conduct and Bodhisattvas performed their practices, which are most supreme;
or on the fifteenth day of the first month, which is also a most excellent time."
If one receives a mantra from a preceptor and first undergoes the period of service (*sevā*), one should then maintain it through recitation; before long, success will be swiftly attained.
Alternatively, if one sees the Lord of Mantras in a dream and is instructed by him, one will likewise achieve swift accomplishment by following those instructions.

"If that practitioner of recitation increases their offerings at a particularly exalted site, or applies even greater sincerity during the specific time, then because of this excellence alone—even if the required number has not been reached—the Lord of Mantras will be pleased and grant accomplishment."
One should know that although the siddhi of this dharma is swift, it will soon perish; for this reason, that which is obtained after first completing the ritual service is said to be firm and stable.

During the initial period of service, one should perform extensive offerings; furthermore, during solar and lunar eclipses, as well as on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar month, one should present additional offerings to the assembly of ṛṣis and devas, as described in other sections.
"On the aforementioned days, one should perform various virtuous deeds and observe fasts and precepts; furthermore, one should increase the offerings to the principal deity of the mantra.
On that day, one should fill a flask with scented water and insert flower branches into it;
or, taking an *argha* vessel, one should empower it by reciting the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra, and by sprinkling it upon one's own head, one can eliminate demonic obstacles."
On that day, one must additionally offer various foods and drinks, as well as apply ointments to the maṇḍala, perform homa, light lamps, and so forth.

In some rites, it is taught that natural signs will appear through mere recitation; if the painted cloth, the image, or the śarīra stūpa shakes or emits flames and light before one, one should know that accomplishment will soon be swiftly attained.
"When accomplishment is attained, what are its signs?
They are as follows:
the body becomes light and agile, and the suffering of illness is forever eliminated;..."
Supreme wisdom increases and the mind is free from fear;
the majestic radiance of the body manifests as courageous strength;
and in dreams at night, one constantly sees pure and true matters, while the mind remains perpetually peaceful and secure.
One should not give rise to weariness while reciting mantras or performing ritual activities;
one should emit a wondrous fragrance from the body, or practice courageous giving and show reverence to those who are venerable and virtuous;
and one should develop deep respect and admiration for the Lord of Mantras.
When these signs appear at the time of accomplishment, one should know that they are the very marks of success.
Once the preliminary rites are concluded, one should worship the Honored One according to the ritual rules, and further increase the offerings and perform homa.

Once the preliminary service according to the prescribed number has been completed, one must next perform the recitation for *siddhi*, first making a prayer to seek the desired signs within one's dreams.

"When performing the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should achieve *siddhi* at the very place where one intends to recite; the recitation must not be moved to another location. If obstacles arise and one wishes to move, one must again perform the preliminary service at the new dwelling before proceeding with the *siddhi*-recitation."

If one does not rely on the aforementioned recitation, one should undergo a purificatory rite (daṇḍa): one must cause [the practitioner] to take up the mantra of the Lord of the Family and recite it one thousand times, or otherwise recite the root-holding mantra (mūladhāraṇī) one hundred thousand times. If one departs from this, one must again perform the preliminary service (sevā) as previously described.
While reciting with right mindfulness, if one suddenly errs and recites another mantra, upon realizing the mistake, one should sincerely repent:
"Due to negligence, this error has occurred; I pray that the Honored One will forgive this transgression."
Then, having prostrated with the crown of the head, one must again recite [the mantra] from the beginning.

If, due to mental negligence while in an impure place, one recites the root mantra, one should immediately recognize this and undergo purification. Upon returning to the place of recitation, one should recite the King of the Family Mantra seven times; for half a month, one day every half-month, one shall fast and consume the five purities (*pañcagavya*). Having recited the mantra of the five purities eight hundred times, one may then consume them.
By wearing these five purifiers, whatever impure or foul food has been consumed during the half-month shall become purified, and the power of the mantra will increase.
The Five Purifier Mantra of the Buddha Family is as follows:
*Namo bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya viśuddhe virājite śive śāntike kare svāhā.* The Five Purifier Mantra of the Lotus Family is as follows:
"Oṃ yaśuśe svāhā. The mantra for the five purifications of the Vajra family is: "Namo ratnatrayāya..."
Oṃ śamśamana-vajra-pāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpate.
Oṃ śiri śiri ṇi ra maṅgala.
Pravipravasavaṃdeśi.
"Oṃ devadevi prabhāve svāhā. Take the milk, curd, ghee, dung, and urine of a yellow cow;

recite the mantra over each separately eight hundred times and place them together in one spot. Then, for another eight hundred times, place them in a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, or in a leaf from a milky tree, or in an *argha* vessel. Stir them with *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra one hundred times. Afterward, squatting and facing east, drink three *akṣa* measures at once; repeat this three times.
Just as when mixing medicinal decoctions, one should not speak while taking them;

so too, when reciting mantras, if an image appears or a voice speaks, one must first exercise discernment. One should immediately recite the mantra and perform the mudrā of the Lord of the Family (Kuladevatā); if it is a māra, it will naturally withdraw.
Or, if the speech that emerges differs from the original rite, one should know it to be the work of a māra.
Or if one utters speech that encourages the commission of evil deeds, one should likewise recognize this as Māra.
If one has a bad dream, one must first recite the mantra of the Mother of the Family (Kulamātṛ) one hundred times;
if one does not first recite the mantra of the Mother of the Family, one must not perform the recitation.
When reciting, one must not cease even if the count falls short; there is no fault in increasing it.
One must strictly follow the sequence of recitation as described above;
if one deviates from this method while seeking *siddhi*, it cannot be attained.

19. Chapter on the Ritual for Manifesting Radiance (*Prabhāsvara-vidhi*) The Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Nineteen: The Ritual for Manifesting Radiance "Furthermore, I shall now explain the ritual for augmenting majestic power and causing [the deities] to rejoice, whereby the mantras one upholds will be swiftly accomplished."

First, having bathed the body and head with scented water, one should perform various offerings on a major festival day. Then, taking one hundred *sumana* flowers, one should recite the mantra over each individual flower twenty-one times, seven times, or three times.
First, observe the number of syllables in the mantra and recite it as an offering to the deity;
next, offer unguents and incense, especially those of extraordinary fragrance;
then offer food and drink, adding sugar and curd as previously described.
Perform the homa again, using only that wood to burn; do not exceed the prescribed measure, burning one hundred and eight pieces.
Next, perform the homa one hundred and eight times using milk curd mixed with honey.
Next, perform the homa one hundred and eight times using ghee and curd mixed with cooked non-glutinous rice, for twenty-one days, or seven days, or even three mornings.
Once these three are completed, one should take milk porridge mixed with cow’s ghee and perform homa one hundred and eight times;
when this is finished, take an arghya vessel, recite the mantra over it one hundred and eight times, pour a small amount of water into it, and perform homa.
"When performing these dharmas, the mantras become more powerful; even if their majesty is interrupted by other mantras, they may still attain increase;
or if the mantras are damaged, they may still attain increase;
or if the mantras are intercepted and do not function..."
Or it may be bound;
or the mantras may be mutually intermingled;
or the mantras may have missing syllables.
Alternatively, if the syllables of the mantra increase, all such afflictions as mentioned above will be entirely eliminated and its majestic power will increase.
"In any of the homa rites, take one of the medicinal herbs described therein and perform the homa for one day and night; the mantra will become joyful and its majestic power will increase."

Furthermore, take various fragrances and blend them to form a fragrant paste, fashioning the form of the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Offer *tala-tṛ* flowers and burn resin incense or hard-wood incense. Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times during each of the three periods of the day; thus, the mantra will be pleased and its power increased.

Fashion this form of the Honored One and place it upon a lotus leaf, or a plantain leaf, or a leaf from a milk-tree, or upon various grass leaves; offer it not only by day but also by night. When the ritual is completed, dispatch it according to the rite and set it adrift upon a great river.
If one performs [the rites] according to this sequence and these rules, the deity will be pleased and swiftly bestow *siddhi*.

Chapter Twenty: The Ritual for Consecrating the Deity (*Abhiṣeka-devatā-vidhi-paṭala*) from the Susiddhikara-sūtra. "Furthermore, once the preliminary services have been completed, if one wishes to increase the majesty and power of the mantra-lord, one should consecrate him."
Take a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or a new earthenware jar, fill it with scented water, and place within it the five precious gems, flowers, fruits, and fragrant leaves.

Furthermore, setting aside the five grains, various unguents, or powdered incense, one should tie a new piece of colored silk around the neck of the flask, insert branches of *tāla* trees or milky sap trees, and recite either the mantra of the Lord of the Family or the mantra of the Mother of the Family one hundred and eight times; thereafter, one should consecrate the crown of the head of the Lord of the Mantra.
One should fashion its form using gold and the like, as well as *agaru* (sandalwood) and *candana* (sandalwood), place it upon a seat, and perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Once the consecration is completed, one should further present offerings such as flowers, incense, colored cloths, or various necklaces; one should worship it with these diverse ritual implements. For the sake of making this offering, one should again perform *homa* and add recitation (*japa*). By acting in this manner, one can cause the deity to increase in power and swiftly attain *siddhi*.
"When performing recitation following a prior ritual service, one should consecrate the deity by taking an *argha* vessel and visualizing the deity while bestowing the empowerment;
or, when one has finished bathing oneself, one should again visualize the Lord of Mantras and empower him three or seven times."

One should not neglect or forget the prior service; alternatively, one may fill a flask with milk, or clarified butter (*sarpis*), or honey, and according to the ritual, place within it seven precious jewels and other items for the consecration of the *iṣṭadevatā*. Thus, the prayed-for aspiration will swiftly be fulfilled.
Chapter 21: Signs of the Efficacy of Prayers. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-one: Signs of the Efficacy of Prayers. "Furthermore, the rules for the rite of prayer shall be explained in detail."
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, as well as on the days of solar and lunar eclipses, one should fast for one day;

or for three days, or for seven days. Having bathed for purification and donned fresh, clean garments, one should perform the invocation from the following morning. For such invocations, one should use the *śāntika* mantra during the waxing moon to make the petition.

Furthermore, at dusk, one should bathe with various medicinal decoctions and use mantras to purify oneself, removing all impurities and sprinkling water upon the five places [of the body]. One should then make offerings according to the ritual to the primary mantra-lord;
furthermore, offer arghya while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.

Next, take *jāti* flowers that have not yet fully blossomed, sprinkle them with sandalwood incense, and present them as an offering; moreover, extensively offer food known as *uṇḍerī*, which contains curdled milk (*peyā*) added within it.
Offer a garland made of *maṅlati* flowers.
First, perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings using cow ghee;
next, perform another one hundred and eight *homa* offerings using *sāñjarasa*.
Have a young girl twist together threads of white cotton or cloth threads to form seven knots, reciting the mantra once for each knot.

When the seven knots are completed, recite the mantra seven more times and tie them upon the left upper arm. Then, lying on your right side, contemplate the Lord of Mantras. Once you have received his permission to proceed or cease, remain as you please; seat yourself upon a mat of *kuśa* grass, scatter flowers, and visualize the form of the Honored One.
"If, within that dream, one sees the lord of one's own family,
or the lord of mantras,
or sees a vidyārāja, one should know that this sign is a sign of accomplishment."
One may see the Three Jewels;
or various bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, as well as the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*) for those who make offerings;
or one may see oneself reciting and upholding mantras while performing various rites.
Or one may see oneself wearing pure white garments;
or again, seeing others come to make offerings, one should know that the supreme *siddhi* is near.
Or one may see oneself ascending a mountain peak.
Some see themselves riding elephants;
some crossing great rivers and seas;
some climbing fruit trees.
Some ride upon lions;
some upon oxen, deer, horses, or other various beasts;
and some ride upon flying geese, peacocks, birds, and all manner of winged creatures.
One may see a beautiful woman adorned with necklaces and holding a flower vase;
or one may walk along a path surrounded by fragrant flowers and canopies;
or one may receive in a dream elephants, horses, chariots, and various precious objects—seeing such signs constitutes the sign of *siddhi*.
"Alternatively, dreaming of obtaining flowers, fruits, roots, ghee, milk, curd, rice-powder, or similar items are signs of the *siddhi* of the medicinal substances to be accomplished.

During the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), if one dreams of these accomplished medicines or obtains a rosary, one who obtains such signs should know that they must immediately perform the recitation ritual (*japa-vidhi*). Or, one may see oneself being perfumed with incense;
or one may see oneself bathing and becoming pure."

Alternatively, if one sees oneself wearing necklaces and ornaments upon the body, having seen this sign, one should perform recitation and will swiftly attain *siddhi*. Regarding the method for performing recitation:
take one hundred *jāti* flowers and, using the *kula-mātṛ-mantra* together with the root mantra, recite them in unison one hundred and eight times as an offering.

Furthermore, take white sandalwood incense and recite the mantra over it one hundred times; by making such supplications, you shall obtain whatever you desire. When you lie down to sleep, the Lord of Mantras will manifest a sign to you of his own accord.

Alternatively, take the *uśīra* herb, pound it, and fashion it into the form of the Lord of Mantras. Using soil from an anthill (*ulmīka*) mixed with earth, fashion a vessel, fill it with cow’s milk, and place the image within.

Or, using clarified butter, milk, and honey mixed together, place them in a vessel and set the image inside. Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and perform offerings at the three periods of the day. By offering in this manner, the Honored One will be pleased and a sign will swiftly appear.

Furthermore, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, as well as on the day of a lunar eclipse and so forth, one should abstain from food, observe the fast, and perform offerings. Using the seven resinous incenses (*gavya-gandha*) and the five solid incenses (*khara-gandha*), for each type of incense, one should recite the mantra once and perform one *homa* offering. Once the count reaches one thousand two hundred times, the signs of the desired vow will swiftly appear.

As extensively explained above regarding the rules for supplication, if one performs them according to the ritual, accomplishment will be swiftly attained; seeing these signs, one should have no doubt.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Ritual for Receiving Mantras from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, the ritual for receiving mantras shall be explained in detail.

Kneeling with both knees upon the ground, first perform extensive acts of giving before the Venerable Ācārya. Holding exquisite flowers in your hands and generating a heart of earnest devotion, receive the mantra orally from the Ācārya three times. As for those who receive more than this, they must not use paper or yellow ox-gall to transcribe it; having received it, they may recite it as they please.

"Once one has already entered the maṇḍala, if at a later time one receives the mantra, one should perform extensive offerings before a venerable ācārya or similar authority on an auspicious day and receive it as previously described. By receiving the mantra in this correct manner, it will be swiftly accomplished; even if one does not perform the preliminary service (puraścaraṇa), one may achieve accomplishment simply by maintaining the recitation."

Furthermore, using a new jar that is free from cracks or defects, place within it flowers, leaves, the seven precious gems, and the five grains, each according to the ritual rules; do not add water, and with a heart of utmost sincerity, perform extensive offerings.

The Ācārya first writes down the names of the various mantra-lords on slips of paper and places them inside a flask, performing the adornment and offerings according to the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
While performing this rite, he shall observe the fast and maintain the precepts for either one day or three days without eating.

If one performs this rite at twilight, one should take *gorocanā* (cow bezoar), write the names of the various mantras upon it, and place them inside a flask. One should then offer it with unguents, flowers, incense, and food, while performing *homa*. Reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should extensively and diligently petition the assembly of noble ones to grant their protective attention.

When three days have thus passed, one should have the disciple take a single leaf from the flask. First, the disciple must bathe his body until it is fragrant, place a *śrīvatsa* (auspicious) ring upon his hand, and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Holding the flask and fumigating it with incense, he should prostrate himself with a devoted heart and take a leaf;
having taken it, he prostrates again. One who receives [the teaching] in this manner will swiftly attain *siddhi*.

If, however, one recites other mantras instead, the *siddhi* of the mantra received will be lost. If the teacher feels joy toward the disciple, he may grant him the *siddhi-mantra* he himself maintains; the disciple should receive it according to the ritual rules and the Dharma. Because he has first recited and held it, the disciple shall attain *siddhi* before long.
First, one should offer a petition to the Lord of Mantras, saying:
"I bestow this mantra upon this disciple; I pray that you grant your empowerment and swiftly bestow siddhi."
Holding incense and flowers in his hands, he recites [the mantra] one hundred or one thousand times, then calls his disciple and hands them over to him.
He further says:
"At this moment, I transfer the Fundamental Wisdom Lord to you, my disciple; I pray only that you will take notice and grant me *siddhi*."
The disciple should say:
"I have now received the Illustrious Master; I vow that from this day forth until I attain Bodhi, I shall never neglect or forget [the teachings].
As stated above, when the master and disciple receive the mantra-dharma in this manner, they shall surely attain accomplishment (*siddhi*); those who receive it otherwise shall not obtain *siddhi*.
Having thus received the *siddhi-mantra*, one will certainly achieve accomplishment therein without doubt.
Since there is no preliminary service required for a mantra that already possesses *siddhi*, the same applies to the methods for receiving *siddhi* medicines and so forth.

Furthermore, there may be someone who first serves [the deity], and subsequently, having combined recitation and mental retention (*dhāraṇī*), transfers it to another according to the ritual rules; the one who receives it does not first perform service, but attains accomplishment simply by performing recitation and mental retention.

"Those who receive the mantra, for the sake of attaining *siddhi*, should first extensively offer to their preceptor flowers, fruits, medicinal roots, renowned garments and fine robes, gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, various miscellaneous jewels, diverse grains and wheat, jars filled with excellent curd, male and female servants, various bedding, marvelous leather sandals, ornaments for the body, already perfected medicines, elephants, horses, oxen, calves, and other vehicles—even offering one's own person as a servant to be employed. Having served for a long time without fearing toil or hardship, they should reverently and respectfully offer these with palms joined in devotion; by practicing such giving, they will swiftly attain *siddhi*."
As extensively explained above regarding these various items, one must first offer them as gifts to the *upādhyāya* before receiving the sublime phrases of the mantra.

Chapter Twenty-Three: The Chapter on the Ritual for Fulfilling Mantras from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, if the practitioner sees the body of the mantra-lord (*mantrādhipati*) with its various limbs augmented within a dream, it should be known that the syllables of the mantra are augmented;
if the limbs are diminished, it should be known that the syllables are deficient. Having thoroughly understood these signs, one should perform the ritual for fulfillment."

If one perceives that the mantra differs from what was received and upheld—whether by having more or fewer syllables—and doubt arises in the mind, one should perform the rite of fulfillment (*pūraṇa*).

To perform this rite of fulfillment: first, using paper and ox-gall (*gorocanā*), write out the erroneous mantra in a fine hand. Then, according to the ritual rules, make offerings to the Mantra King and protect oneself, and place the mantra upon the seat of the Lord of Mantras.

Furthermore, take the fuel sticks and follow the original ritual manual; however, use only clarified butter (ghṛta) as an auxiliary for seeking the assistance of the Vidyārāja, and thus one should perform the homa.
Spread *kuśa* grass as a mat and first pay homage to the Lord of the Family;
next, pay homage to the Mother of the Family.
Next, he prostrates before all the Buddhas and makes this petition:
"I pray that all Buddhas and all the holy ones will grant their protection and assistance.
Having made this petition, he lies down upon the kusha grass with his head toward the east.

Within the dream, the tutelary deity manifests signs; upon the paper inscribed with ox-gall, there may be additions or omissions, yet the deity re-inscribes it with ox-gall until the annotations are complete, even correcting every added or missing stroke. Thus, the mantra is not erroneous—though one might simply say it is not erroneous—or else the deity provides full instruction within the dream.
When performing this rite, one should perform protective rites for the purpose of eliminating māras.

Chapter Twenty-Four: Increasing Power. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Four: "Furthermore, in order to increase one's power, one should perform homa, using either ghee and honey, or at times using milk;
each of these should be performed separately."
Alternatively, perform homa using sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
or perform homa using resin incense mixed with ghee;
or perform homa using lotus flowers mixed with ghee.
At times, one may use *sajjārāsa*;

or, dwelling among the mountains, one may constantly consume the five pure substances (*pañcāmṛta*) and abstain from all other food. Taking one hundred thousand flowers of the specific deity’s family, reciting the mantra once for each flower, one should offer excellent unguents, incense, flowers, lamps, and food to the tutelary deity. Reciting the mantra eight hundred times for each offering, three times a day for three days, such worship increases the power [of the mantra].
Alternatively, one may burn hard wood as a lamp, three times a day for seven days, which can cause the mantra’s power to increase.
Alternatively, when performing the practice, making offerings of *kāmika* food also increases its power.
Furthermore, the aforementioned rules for recitation, *homa*, and offering likewise enable one to increase its power.

Chapter Twenty-Five: The Rules for Homa. From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Five: The Rules for Homa. "Furthermore, the rules for homa shall be explained in detail, so that the practitioner may swiftly attain siddhi."
In front of the honored image, construct a homa hearth one cubit square; it should have a rim on all four sides and a depth of half a cubit, and the same applies if it is made circular.

If the place for recitation is inside a room, one should go outside and dig the hearth so that it overlooks the form of the honored deity, performing it according to the ritual rules in accordance with the specific rite at hand.

Place items such as milk-wood and fragrant flowers to the right, and the homa vessels to the left. Sprinkle all the materials with the *sarvakarmika-mantra*, sit upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, and compose the mind in meditative concentration. Holding an *argha* vessel, invoke the Lord of Mantras; pour a small amount of the *argha* water into the hearth, and then offer one flower while reciting the mantra once for each to present it to the Lord of Mantras.
To eliminate impurities, one should recite the Kilikili mantra and perform its mudrā;
for protection, one should recite the Kuṇḍalī mantra, sprinkle water for purification, and thereafter kindle the fire with wood from milky trees.
Once the fire has been kindled, first invite the Fire Deity:
"I now respectfully invite the foremost of the Fire Deities, the sage among gods, who is honored by those who practice the holy life; please descend to this place and accept this homa offering."
Next, recite the mantra.
The mantra for summoning the Fire Deity (Agni) is as follows:

“Oṃ jhiḥ hā mahābhūta-nirvāśiṇe viyajasatva-maṃ maṃkṣihṛdaya-hūti mahāhara maśmin saṃnihitopava āgnyaye haye kavyayavahutiye svāhā. Having summoned the Fire Deity, first purify [the offerings] by sprinkling *argha* water three times. Taking various five-grains, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), curd (*dadhi*), and other substances, recite the mantra three times while performing the *homā* fire sacrifice to offer them to the Fire Deity.
The mantra for the fire-god Agni is:

*Āgneye havye kavye vahanaye nibhye nibhye nipathe svāhā*. Having offered the food to the fire-god, one should mentally visualize drawing the fire-god and placing him upon his original seat. Then, reciting the Kṛtikiḷi mantra and performing the hand gesture (*mudrā*), one should purify the fire once more; all *homā* (fire-offerings) should be performed in this manner.
Next, invite the Principal Deity (iṣṭadevatā). First, recite the mantra of the Principal Deity once and take your seat;
having made offerings according to the ritual rules, [the deity] will graciously accept the homa. Regarding the wood required for the time of the homa, they are:
*plakṣa* wood, *udumbara* wood, *bhallātaka* wood, *nyagrodha* wood, *khadira* wood, *arka* wood, *vikaṅkata* wood, *amra* wood, *kaśmīraja* wood, *śami* wood, *apāmārga* wood, and *aśvattha* wood.
The twelve kinds of tree branches mentioned above should each measure two fingers and one *vitasti* in length and must be moist.

Those freshly gathered may be used for all types of *homa* rites. One should examine the straightness of the branches from top to bottom, place them uniformly, and wash them clean with scented water. The fine tips should point outward and the coarse bases toward the body; dip both ends in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and cast them into the fire-pit.

When performing rites such as śāntika and others, one should follow the specific procedure of each respective rite; first, one should offer a ball of food (piṇḍa) as a homa, and this ritual pattern applies universally to all.

"When preparing food each day, first set aside one portion of the meal and place it before the Honored One; this should be used first when performing homa. When reciting mantras, hold the food with both hands between the knees; the same should be done during homa."

Take four finger-widths of *śamī* wood, as thick as the index finger, and perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings with ghee mixed with incense; this rite is profound and subtle, enhancing the power of mantras, and when performed in this manner, it is universally applicable to all *kulas*.
Alternatively, one may perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings using *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter;
or at times, one may perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings using *agaru* alone. All of these are capable of augmenting the power and efficacy of the mantra.

"If one performs various homas for the sake of accomplishing the mantra-dharma, one should first invite the Lord of the Family, then invite the Principal Deity (iṣṭadevatā), and thereafter perform the homa according to the ritual rules;

if one performs various homas for the sake of accomplishing the mantra-dharma, one should first use the mantra of the Family Mother to protect the Principal Deity and then oneself, and thereafter perform the homa according to the ritual rules;

if one performs various homas for the sake of accomplishing the mantra-dharma, at the conclusion of the homa, for the purpose of augmenting the power of the mantra, one should recite the Family Heart-mantra."

In order to accomplish the various mantra-rites, whenever one performs any homa, at the beginning one must always use the large ladle to draw and offer the oblation; when about to conclude, one should likewise use the large ladle to pour out three full libations, while during the intervening period, the small ladle should be employed.
To accomplish the mantra-rites, upon finishing the homa, one should use the Family Heart Mantra (kula-hṛdaya-mantra) to recite over the arghya water and present it as an offering.
"As it is taught in the maṇḍala rites regarding homa, the sequence for requesting the performance of homa should be likewise.
First perform the ābhicāruka rite;
next perform the pauṣṭika rite."
Furthermore, perform the śāntika rite.
Once the homa is completed, empower pure water with the mantra of the deity and sprinkle it into the hearth while circling around it with the hand.

When these three rounds of homa are completed, once again address the Fire Deity to receive the remaining offerings. Retire and dismiss him according to the ritual, substituting the word for "departure" (*visarjana*) for the word for "descent" (*āhvāna*) used in the invocation. Combine the remaining grains, ghee, honey, curd, and so forth into one place, and perform homa by reciting the mantra of the aforementioned Fire Deity three times.
Furthermore, recite the root mantra according to its syllabic length;
then perform offerings and provide protection for the deity and for yourself, dismissing them according to the ritual.

Chapter Twenty-Six: On the Preparation of the Requisites for Recitation. The Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Six: On the Preparation of the Requisites for Recitation. "Furthermore, the various requisites for accomplishment shall be explained in detail."
In order to accomplish all mantras, one should first prepare various miscellaneous items and subsequently perform the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*).
Having completed the preliminary service, one should then engage in recitation, namely:
various types of unguents, incenses, and so forth.
"The five kinds of solid fragrances are:
aloeswood, sandalwood, red sandalwood, sālā-fragrance, and celestial wood fragrance, etc.
The seven resinous fragrances are:"
Gandharasa incense, sārjarasa incense, guggulu incense, spṛkkā incense, turuṣka incense, śallakī incense, and śrīveṣṭaka incense.
As well as white mustard seeds, poison, *bṛhatī* seeds, sesame oil, cow’s ghee, a flask, and a copper bowl.
The five grains are:
barley, wheat, rice, small beans, and sesame.
"The five treasures are:
gold, silver, pearls, conch shells, and red pearls.
The five medicines are:"
The medicinal herb *khaṇḍakāri*, the medicinal herb *vṛhantī*, the medicinal herb *saha*, the medicinal herb *sahadeva*, and the medicinal herb *śvetagirikarṇikā*.
"The Five-Colored Thread" refers to blue, yellow, red, white, and black.

The thread spun by a young girl, a vajra, a lamp wick, a lamp bowl, a clay vessel, five types of colored pigments, a *keta-ra* wooden peg, a branch of milky sap wood, a bowl of *kṛtavedhana* wood, a large ladle, a small ladle, cow bezoar, high-carbon steel, red sandalwood, a consecrated thread (*pavitraka*), a pure bathing robe, a black deerskin, *bhr̥ṅgarāja* flowers, *sugandhikā* flowers, wooden sandals, *śara* grass, *darbha* grass, *śatapuṣpā* (fennel/anise), a flower basket for gathering blossoms, and various items required for food and drink such as clarified butter, honey, granulated sugar, and rock sugar; the rosary is as described above.
One should prepare all the various items mentioned, and then perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and extensive recitation (*japa*).

Chapter Twenty-Seven: Signs of Accomplishing the Various Items. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Seven: Signs of Accomplishing the Various Items. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the objects for accomplishment; based upon these objects, the *mantra-siddhi* is attained."
They are as follows:
the cintāmaṇi jewel, the auspicious vase, the rain of jewels, the hidden treasure, the wheel, the yellow orpiment, and the sword.

These seven objects are the most supreme among the supreme; they can bring about the accomplishment of various siddhis, increase merit and virtue, and even lead to the fulfillment of the fruit of the Dharma King—how much more so regarding other worldly matters?

The mantras of these three families—the Buddha Family, the Lotus Family, and the Vajra Family—all possess such supreme accomplishments; by selecting and upholding any one among them, one attains the five supernatural powers as the highest siddhi.

"The seven items previously mentioned are now further detailed: one should fashion a golden pedestal, or one made of silver, measuring one cubit in length, adorned with exquisite craftsmanship and set with *maṇi* jewels. It should be embellished with *maṇi*, red glass, and pure, unclouded light, or fine crystal placed upon the top of the pedestal. One who would accomplish this rite should recite the mantra at night, following the pattern for the pedestal as described."

“If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the Worthy Vase (bhadraghaṭa), one should adorn the vase as described in the ‘Chapter on Receiving Mantras,’ with the sole exception that it is not filled with water and is placed upon a bannered pedestal.”
Next, fashion the form of a flask according to the rules for the seal.

If one wishes to accomplish the rite for raining down treasures, once the efficacy of the rite has been realized, by merely maintaining a sincere heart, gold, silver, and various miscellaneous jewels can be made to rain within a radius of five *yojanas*.

"If one wishes to accomplish the dharma of hidden treasures, once the efficacy of the rite has been realized, one need only maintain a sincere heart; wherever one directs one's thoughts, hidden treasures will manifest. With a storehouse filled with pure gold, one shall provide for the poor and destitute, and though used for various expenses, the treasury will never be exhausted."

"If one wishes to accomplish the Wheel-Rishi (*cakravartin*) rite, one should fashion a wheel from tempered steel (*vaidūrya*), measuring two fingers and one span (*vitasti*) in circumference; the wheel should have six spokes and a rim that is fine and sharp. By practicing according to this method, one will swiftly attain *siddhi*."

"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of realgar (*haritāla*), first take high-quality, radiant realgar that is like the light of the newly risen sun; its glowing smoke is crimson, just like refined gold. When it is turned into water, it has the luster of molten gold and smoky light—one should take such excellent realgar as this."

"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the sword, first take a blade of tempered steel (*vimala*), measuring two cubits in length and four finger-widths in width at the hilt, as broad as the little finger. It must be free from blemishes or spots, and its color should be deep blue, like the feathers of a *saṃśī* bird."
"If one wishes to accomplish the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa rite, one should fashion the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa out of gold, like a painted seal, and place it upon a banner-stand with a shaft made of vaidūrya."
"If one wishes to accomplish the Lotus Dharma, first fashion a lotus flower out of gold; let the flower have eight petals and measure two finger-widths or one span."
It may be made of silver;
or made of refined copper;
or made of white sandalwood.

"If one wishes to accomplish the Vajra, first fashion a *khaṭvāṅga* out of high-carbon steel (*bhallātaka-ayasa*), sixteen finger-widths in length, with three prongs at both ends; or fashion it from red sandalwood;
or fashion it from the three metals—the three metals being gold, silver, and refined copper."

"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of realgar, first take realgar that is the color of gold leaf, consisting of solid pieces yet possessing a radiant luster; such realgar can accomplish this supreme matter."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of ox-gallstone (gorocanā), one should take the gallstone of a yellow cow.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the kairika herb, it is best to first take that herb which is the color of a datura flower."
"If you wish to accomplish the *sru-ta* (suluta) *añjana* medicine, it is best if it resembles the excrement of an earthworm.
If you wish to accomplish a white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), take one that is fine and soft, remove all hair and down, and dye it with *vairāja* gold."
"If one wishes to accomplish the protection cord (*rakṣāsūtra*), take threads of white cotton, triple them three times, and all must be joined from right to left, or else use gold thread."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the flower garland (*mālā*), a young girl should spin the thread, and one should take *jāti* flowers to make the garland.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of cow-dung ash, one should take dried cow dung from a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) and burn it to produce white ash, which is then mixed with camphor."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the wooden sandals, one should take *śrīphala* wood to fashion the sandals and place a lid upon them."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the parasol, the canopy should be made from peacock feathers, and its shaft from fresh, high-quality bamboo.

If one wishes to accomplish the rites for bows, arrows, spears, lances, single-pronged tridents, clubs, or any other weapons, they should each be fashioned according to the common usage of worldly people."
"If one wishes to accomplish worldly objects—

namely, saddled horses, carriages, oxen, sheep, all birds and beasts, and other such things— according to what is collectively esteemed as superior by the people of the world, or according to what one personally desires, or based on the original rite, one should perform the ritual formation in this manner."

"If one wishes to accomplish the Vetāla, one should take the corpse of one born of a noble family, who died suddenly in the prime of life without illness and whose body is free of scars; having taken such a corpse—before it has begun to bloat and while the sense organs remain intact—one should perform the accomplishment."
The success—whether superior, middling, or inferior—is achieved according to what has been performed; the objects to be taken are likewise so.
One should perform this rite only when the mind is free from fear.
28. Chapter on Taking the Objects for Accomplishment, *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: "Furthermore, I shall now explain the method for taking the objects."
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, during solar or lunar eclipses, or on days when an earthquake occurs—one should collect the substances before midday;
or, having attained a meditative state (*viṣaya*) during recitation (*japa*), one should then collect the substances;
or, having bathed for purification, abstained from food, and observed the fast, one should seek a favorable meditative state and collect the substances.
Regarding the necessary items mentioned, one should purchase them from wherever they may be found; one must not take such goods without paying their price.
Alternatively, at times when one perceives an increase in one's own power and is able to endure hunger, cold, and various other hardships, it is at such a time that one may take those goods.

Regarding the various objects to be taken, each according to its inherent nature—whether superior, middling, or inferior—one should select those of the highest quality; having obtained them in accordance with the Dharma, one should apply diligent effort to perform the rite of accomplishment.
Chapter 29: Purification of All Substances from the Susiddhikara Sūtra Furthermore, I shall now explain the method for purifying all substances by means of sprinkling.

First, wash it with the five purifiers; for those parts that should not be washed, sprinkle them with the five purifiers. Observe the proportions of the yellow arsenic (雌黃) as one would for the five purifiers, and then grind them together into a powder.
Make a powder of realgar mixed with milk;

Chapter Thirty-one: The Ritual of the Great Consecration Maṇḍala for the Removal of All Obstacles from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, I shall extensively explain the secret and wondrous rites for accomplishing all substances, so that *siddhi* may be swiftly attained."

If one wishes to begin the practice of the *sādhana*, one should first prepare all the requisites for *siddhi*; next, one should empower the mantra of the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and perform self-consecration by means of the rite of *homa*.

One who desires to receive initiation should construct a maṇḍala and perform offerings according to the ritual; having performed the initiation, one may then begin the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Next, the great maṇḍala of initiation is explained, which is capable of accomplishing all matters. All methods previously described for the maṇḍala of the Vidyārāja, such as the purification of the site and so forth, should be performed in this same manner.

That maṇḍala is square with four corners and four gates arranged at the cardinal points; its dimensions are eight cubits, or seven, or five. Only the four gates are opened, and the boundary lines are clearly demarcated, painted with five colors according to the pattern of a calyx. "To the west of this, four cubits away, construct another maṇḍala measuring five, four, or three cubits.
Open only the eastern gate, or make it half the size of the location for the consecration in the fundamental great maṇḍala."
In general, the terrain of a maṇḍala must slope toward the entrance so that water drains out; this is said to be auspicious.
However, a maṇḍala whose terrain slopes toward the north is said to be the most excellent.
"Alternatively, one may paint it using a single color; at the four corners, draw trident-vajras (triśūla-vajra);
within the central platform, draw an eight-petaled lotus according to the ritual rules. All maṇḍalas should be executed in this manner."
Around the perimeter outside the lotus petals, draw auspicious and wondrous seals;

furthermore, place auspicious vases at all the corners, and do likewise for the outer initiation maṇḍala.

"Those who wish to perform the consecration must have four types [of vessels]. The locations for placing the vases should be at the corners of the boundary lines. According to the mantras and vidyās being recited, one should draw the seal (mudrā) of the principal deity within the platform and place a vase there. For the mantra being recited, one should draw the seal of the presiding deity according to its respective family—namely:
Buddha-Usnīṣa, Lotus, and Vajra."

Next, on the outside facing east, draw the seal of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa;
on its right side, the seal of the Family Mother (Kulīśvarī), and on its left side, the seal of the Family Heart (Kulahrdaya).
Next, on the right, place the seal of Śāriputra; next, on the left, the seal of the Tooth;

next, on the right, Ānanda; and next, on the left, Subhūti. All other mantras, vidyās, and so forth, along with their seals, are to be arranged on the left and right, extending even to the two corners.

"On the right side outside the gate of the second maṇḍala, paint the nāga king Nanda; on the left side, paint the nāga king Upananda.
Outside the gates of the third maṇḍala, paint the nāga king Sundara on the right side and the nāga king Upasundara on the left."
Outside the maṇḍala, draw the seal of the amṛta-flask.

To expel the vināyakas, one should perform the abhicāru rite;

"To the noble ones and the various deities assembled in the maṇḍala, one should perform three types of homa, each with their respective root mantras;

"The mantra-holders he carries are placed within the altar maṇḍala beneath the principal deity.

Having thus empowered this superior flask and having made offerings to it, one should next circumambulate it to the right.

32. Chapter on the Manifestation of All Ritual Substances, the Thirty-second of the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, once the ritual consecration has been performed according to the Dharma, one should perform homa for twenty-one days, or seven days, or for one month;
or as corresponds to the specific accomplishment (*sādhana*) at hand.

Either by relying on this very rite;

sprinkle it with water infused with *gorocanā* or white mustard seeds, and on festival days, offer that object along with various ritual implements.
"If it is accomplished during the waxing moon, one should take the fifteenth day;
if it is accomplished during the waning moon, one should take the fourteenth day.
To thus manifest the brilliance of the object, one should employ the mantra of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ) for all such cases."

Furthermore, one should again increase the offerings with various fragrant flowers, garlands, and other articles; having anointed the hands with incense and placed a ring of *kuśa* grass, one should press upon the object to be accomplished and perform recitation throughout the night, chanting one hundred and eight times during each of the three periods of the night.
Such objects manifested through this illumination should be treated in this manner from beginning to end; if one possesses this method, accomplishment will be swiftly attained.

"Alternatively, one may construct a maṇḍala for the purpose of illumination; as previously described for purifying the ground, one constructs a maṇḍala using five colors, measuring four cubits in size and provided with a single gate."

next, in the southern direction, the Vajra Mudrā, with the mudrā of the Māmakī Family Mother placed on its right side.

Furthermore, on the southern side, one should arrange all the retinues belonging to that respective division in their proper order;
however, on the western side, one may place the various mudrās of the three families according to one's preference.

"Next, place the great deities of the eight directions, such as Kuvera and others, in the outer enclosure; in the empty spaces thereof, place at will the lords of the mantras that accomplish all tasks within the three families.

To the east of the object, place the root mantra and the mudrā held by the practitioner; to the west of the object, install the homa fire-pit.
Next, the reciter shall sit to the west, and each shall invoke [the deity] according to their respective root mantra and the prescribed ritual, making offerings in the sequence previously described.

Having completed the offerings, one should perform homa with the vidyās of the three families in succession to illuminate the object, and thereafter perform homa with the root mantra to bring about illumination.

"Among all radiant dharmas, homa is supreme. At the beginning of every homa, one should first recite the Family Mother mantra, sprinkle the substances with scented water to purify them, and likewise sprinkle them when the homa is completed."
Alternatively, one may use the heart-mantra of Mañjughoṣa, or the four-syllable mantra of the Vidyārāja; in all cases, one should perform the homa of the three families to bring about illumination.
When performing the homa with whichever mantra is being used, first recite that mantra, and then recite the words of supplication.
Furthermore, recite its mantra in the middle, and again recite the words of supplication;
then again recite its mantra, placing the words of supplication back within it.
Thus, within this mantra, the words of supplication are placed in three positions—upper, middle, and lower—and finally, the syllables "HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ" are placed. That is to say:

Jva-jvala! Let light radiate! Siddhi-siddhya! Let success be accomplished! Jvala-bhāsa-bhāsana! O you who possess radiant splendor! Tejovati-tejaya! Let brilliance increase! Vardhaya! Let it grow! Mā vilamba! Do not delay! Avīśa! Enter everywhere! Rakṣa! Protect! Sani! Be swift! Svāhā! May auspiciousness appear! Kuru! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!
By means of such phrases of invocation, one should illuminate the object; there is no hindrance to repeating these variously at the beginning, end, or middle.
Once the *homa* is completed, one should next perform recitation (*japa*), scattering white *karavīra* flowers over the object to illuminate it;
or one may recite while holding red *karavīra* flowers.
Alternatively, one may use white mustard seeds;
or one may use sumana flowers to bring forth radiance.
First, apply scented ointment to the hands and press them upon the object; next, hold various flowers while reciting the mantra and scatter them.
Next, scatter white mustard seeds;
next, fumigate it with burning incense;
and finally, recite the mantra while sprinkling scented water.

One should know that following this sequence, during the three periods of the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one should recite the mantra of the principal deity. Having sprinkled [the site] with water consecrated by the perfume-mantra, one should then recite the root-holding mantra. Once the sprinkling is finished, one should perform the homa and recitation as before until sunrise. One who possesses this method will swiftly attain accomplishment.

"In this way, by manifesting all objects as well as one's own body, one will certainly and swiftly attain accomplishment; even if the objects are few, one shall obtain great efficacy. Chapter Thirty-Three: Distinguishing the Times for Attaining Siddhi Furthermore, I shall now explain the auspicious times for attaining accomplishment as they have been taught;
once the practitioner has understood these, he should seek siddhi. As for those times, they are the eighth month, the twelfth month, the first month, the second month, and the fourth month.
During the fifteenth day of the white fortnight of these five months, one should perform the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*).
During the fourth month, there will inevitably be the obstacle of rain;
during the second month, there will likewise be the obstacle of wind.
In the first month, there are various obstacles;
however, in the twelfth month, there are no such difficulties.
In the eighth month, there should be the perils of thunder, hail, and lightning; all the aforementioned obstacles are signs of accomplishment.
During these five months, one should seek only to perform the *sādhana*.

One should also perform the *śāntika* rites; specifically, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight within these five months, one should perform the two methods of middling and lower accomplishment.
Furthermore, one should also perform the *pauṣṭika* and *abhicāruka* rites.
"One should accomplish the most supreme objects during a lunar eclipse;
during a solar eclipse, one may accomplish objects of superior, middling, or inferior grades.
Alternatively, on the fifteenth day of the month, or the seventh, the first, or the thirteenth, or using any three days, one should perform the accomplishments and all other rites."

If one performs the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*), one should select the time of the superior lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and planets (*graha*); it should be understood that the methods for the inferior [accomplishments] follow this same principle.

"Furthermore, among all the lunar mansions, the *Ārdrā* (Ghost) mansion is the most excellent; if one performs a fierce accomplishment (*tīkṣṇasādhana*), one must likewise rely on the times of fierce lunar mansions and planets."
Alternatively, it may correspond with three types of ritual matters (*dharmas*), and its accomplishment is likewise performed based on these three matters; or as described in the root text;
or according to the instructions of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
"Furthermore, from the first to the fifteenth day of the tenth, second, or third month, one should perform all accomplishments (*sādhana*) and rites within that interval.
Alternatively, one may select the lunar day corresponding to the finger-number of the deity;
or one may achieve accomplishment on the thirteenth day of either the waxing or waning moon in any month."
The seventh and eighth months are the latter period of the rainy season; during this time, one should perform *śāntika* rites.
The ninth and tenth months are the early winter period; during this time, one should perform *paustika* rites.
The third and fourth months are the latter period of spring; during this time, one should perform *ābhicāruka* rites.
The first and second months are the initial seasons of spring; at this time, one should accomplish all matters.
The fifth and sixth months are the initial season of the rains; those who wish to achieve results should perform *kṣudrasiddhi* (minor accomplishments) during these months.

In this manner, during the seasons of spring, winter, and after the rains, one should likewise accomplish the three types of *siddhi*. Within these, the nine grades are distributed according to their respective categories.
"When accomplishing the lower grade during the first watch of the night;
when accomplishing [the middle grade] during the middle watch of the night;"
During the latter part of the night, when the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*) is performed;
during the first part of the night, it is the time for performing *śāntika* rites;
and during the middle part of the night, it is the time for performing *abhicāruka* rites.

During the latter part of the night, when performing the *puṣṭika* rite, one should know the appropriate timing by distinguishing these three matters into nine grades according to their respective correspondences; within those time periods, one must discern the superior, middling, and inferior signs that appear.

"However, during solar and lunar eclipses, one should immediately perform the ritual without regard for the specific time of day; for all rites of fierce accomplishment (*tīkṣṇa-sādhana*) and *abhicāruka* (subjugation), the times of solar and lunar eclipse are most appropriate.
When beginning any accomplishment, one should fast for three days, two days, or one day, according to whether the rite is classified as superior, middling, or inferior."

"When constructing a maṇḍala, during recitation, and on festival days, one must always apply eye-salve promptly.

Take equal parts of *sūruta*, *āñjana*, *śarkarā-madhu*, *karpūra*, *pippalī*, *brahmaruṣka*, *devadāru*, and naturally occurring *śarkarā*; grind and sift them into a powder, mix it with the froth from a horse’s mouth, and grind it finely. Then, recite this vidyā over it one hundred times.
At the time of accomplishment, one should wash the face repeatedly and apply the medicinal ointment to the eyes to eliminate sloth and torpor; when obstacles arise, they will all be seen from afar.
The mantra of the Buddha Family is:
