"Oṃ vairocani svāhā. The mantra of the Vajra Family is:
"Oṃ mandalinyai pade svāhā. This mantra of the three families is applicable for all purposes.

If a practitioner who maintains the recitation finds their chanting exhausted when they are about to achieve accomplishment, they should mix white sandalwood with water, recite the Family Heart Mantra over it seven times, and drink three handfuls.
When one wishes to achieve accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should first sprinkle water upon the body and wait for auspicious signs before proceeding with the rite of accomplishment.
These auspicious signs are as follows:

the conch shell, the wheel, the hook, the fish, the clockwise-turning seal (*pradakṣiṇa-mudrā*), the white lotus, the banner, the *svastika* seal, the full vase, the *śrīvatsa* seal, the vajra, and the flower garland.
Sometimes they see beautiful women adorned with necklaces and ornaments;
sometimes they see pregnant women or those carrying clothes and belongings;
or they see joyful young maidens.
Or they may see a pure-practicing Brahmin wearing fresh white robes;
or they may see him riding in a carriage, or on an elephant or horse, or with medicinal roots and fruits;
or they may see some extraordinary occurrence.
Some hear the sound of thunder;
some hear the sound of Vedic recitation;
and some hear the sounds of various musical instruments, such as conchs and horns being blown.
Or they may hear the sounds of auspicious birds such as peacocks, partridges, geese, and parrots;
or they may hear voices of kind words and consolation—words that inaugurate well-being, success, and what is pleasing to the mind;
or they may see celebratory clouds, lightning, gentle breezes, and fine rain.
Either flowers rain down from the heavens;
or there is exquisite fragrance and the appearance of halos and rainbows.
Among these signs, that which involves the descent of celestial flowers constitutes the supreme accomplishment.
Manifestation in space constitutes middling accomplishment;
manifestation on the ground constitutes inferior accomplishment.
Regarding these three signs, they are further distinguished into nine grades. As manifested above, all are auspicious; those who perceive them otherwise do not achieve accomplishment.
Having seen these signs, one should give rise to profound joy; it is with such a mind that one should then perform the accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Chapter 35: Requesting the Honored One’s Empowerment for Accomplishment. From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Five: "Requesting the Honored One’s Empowerment for Accomplishment. Furthermore, the method for respectfully invoking the accomplishment is explained.
The aforementioned times, lunar mansions, and auspicious signs have been explained in detail within the rituals for constructing maṇḍalas and the methods for spiritual accomplishment (*sādhana*).

If unfavorable signs appear, one should immediately perform homa with cow’s ghee using the Mother of the Family mantra one hundred times; thereafter, when performing the ritual, one will also attain the accomplishment of siddhi.
"One should also perform the accomplishment based upon the previously described maṇḍala site:
for a superior accomplishment, one should do so on a mountain;
for a middling accomplishment, one should do so by the side of a pond."
If one seeks lower-level accomplishments, they may be performed anywhere;
however, if one performs them in a place corresponding to a specific mantra, success will be attained there. If one does not rely on such a location, accomplishment will be somewhat delayed.
Within a *caitya* containing bone relics (*śarīra*), all mantras of the Inner Dharma will attain accomplishment.
Among all sites of accomplishment, the eight great *caityas*, such as the place of the Buddha’s birth and so forth, are the most supreme.

However, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there are no obstacles whatsoever that can hinder one’s attainment of accomplishment; even the Māra King cannot create difficulties there, much less other classes of beings.
Therefore, all mantras will certainly achieve accomplishment.
"Whatever fierce accomplishments there may be, they should be performed in a cemetery or in an empty house."
One should perform the rite of accomplishment either in a temple dedicated to a single deity where no others reside,
or beneath a solitary tree in a remote place, or by the side of a river.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of a female yakṣī, perform it in a forest;
if one wishes to accomplish the dharma of a nāga king, perform it by a spring;
if one wishes to accomplish the dharma of wealth and nobility, perform it upon a roof."
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the messenger (dūta), one should perform it at a place where people gather;
if one wishes to accomplish the rite of entering caves, one should perform it within a cave.
This is the secret place for the accomplishment of discernment.

Having determined the site through selection, one should first abstain from food; the ground should be purified according to the ritual for purifying the maṇḍala site, or according to the ritual for the recitation chamber. When the location is thus cleansed, spiritual efficacy is swiftly attained.
First, using the Sarvakarmasiddhi mantra or the Cundā mantra, recite it over white mustard seeds and other substances, scattering them upon the ground to ward off all obstacles.

Take four stakes made of khadira wood, each two finger-widths in length with one end sharpened like a single-pronged vajra. Anoint the stakes with red sandalwood incense and wrap them with crimson thread. Forming a fist with the Vajrakilaya mudrā, recite the mantra one hundred times and drive the stakes into the four corners so that the tips protrude slightly.

Prepare a single white banner and suspend it from long bamboo poles erected to the east and west of the maṇḍala. Recite the Vajraprākāra mantra over iron filings one hundred times and fashion three-pronged vajras joined together to encircle the maṇḍala, serving as the vajra wall.

Furthermore, recite the Vajrāvaraṇa mantra over iron filings one hundred times and likewise fashion three-pronged vajras, each placed horizontally upon the vertical vajras to surround the maṇḍala, serving as the vajra railing.
"The gate of the outer maṇḍala is protected by the mantra of Kuṇḍalī with the vajra-mudrā;
the second enclosure gate is protected by Hārītī;
and the gate of the central platform is protected by Aparājita."
These methods for protecting the gates are applicable to all three families, or alternatively, one may employ a single one to protect all three gates.
These three holy ones can crush all obstacles and cannot be defeated; this is the secret protection for accomplishing the ritual objects.
"At the center of that altar, one should bury the five precious substances and other such items.

However, when constructing a maṇḍala at a place where people gather, these five precious substances and others should not be buried; rather, they should simply be placed beneath the object being fashioned. The same applies when constructing a maṇḍala in a courtyard, within a room, or inside a Buddha hall."
"In these five locations, it is sufficient merely to recite [the mantra] and sprinkle scented water to achieve purification; there is no need to dig the ground.
If one performs this rite within one's own regular recitation chamber, accomplishment will be swiftly attained."
One must certainly not perform the rites of accomplishment within various rooms,
nor should one do so in a dilapidated room.

When one wishes to construct a maṇḍala, during the evening seven days prior, with a mind of reverent devotion, one should visualize the deities as if they were present before one's eyes and address this invitation:

"Within the three families, all the honored ones, as well as the deities and their retinues within this own treasury, I have for a long time performed recitation, homa, and maintained the precepts. With this sincere heart, I make offerings to you, honored ones; I pray that on the seventh day henceforth, you will descend to this ritual arena. Out of compassion for me, please accept these humble offerings and, through your great loving-kindness and compassion, grant me accomplishment."

In this manner, continuing until the seventh day has passed, one should make the request at the appointed time and then perform the ritual. Furthermore, with *argha* water, flowers, incense, food and drink, and hymns of praise, one should make special offerings each evening to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) of one direction; this should be done likewise for all three directions.
Furthermore, one should apply incense to the hands and recite the mantra while pressing those hands upon the object to invoke it;
again, one should invoke it by fumigating the object with burning incense;
and furthermore, one should observe a fast.

Selecting an auspicious day and time, construct a mandala briefly; using articles for invocation or simply employing a single color, create a circular mandala with only one gate opened, placing an eight-petaled lotus in its center measuring two cubits in size, while the remaining outer enclosure may be made of any size as desired.
"First, place the lords of the three families within the inner court. To the north of the western gate, place Maheśvara and his consort.
To the right of the Buddha, place Tejorāśi; to the left, place Buddhalocanā.
Next, to the right of Avalokiteśvara, place Mahāśrī; to the left, place Ṣaḍbhuja."

Next, place Mañjughoṣa on the right side of the Vajra and the Heart Mantra of the Vidyārāja on the left side; at the southern side of the western gate, place the wrathful Kili-Kili and the Vajrāṅkuśa.
All that has been described above should be installed within the inner court.

Next, the deities of the eight directions and the lords of mantras who accomplish all tasks should be placed in the outer court; furthermore, the lords of mantras whom one holds most dear in both the inner and outer courts should all be installed at the outer gate.
Place Kuṇḍalī in the north and Aparājita at the southern gate; invite and make offerings to each with their respective heart-mantras.
Place the articles for accomplishment upon a lotus flower to offer them;
alternatively, place a full kalaśa vessel upon a lotus flower and set the articles for accomplishment upon it.
Alternatively, one may place a casket upon a lotus flower and store the substance within it;
or one may place a lotus flower inside a ceramic vessel and store the substance therein;
or one may place the substance within the calyx of the flower upon the lotus flower, pressing it down with the hand while reciting the mantra over the substance one thousand or one hundred times.
Next, one should again recite the mantra while throwing flowers upon the object;
next, one should burn incense made by blending *guggulu* with clarified butter to fumigate it;
and next, one should lightly sprinkle the object with scented water.

Next, one should again recite the *mūlavidyā* (root mantra) of the Family Mother over the object; for all the deities present in the maṇḍala, one should likewise recite their respective mantras over the object.
Next, perform the homa with cow's ghee;
alternatively, use cow's milk, or a mixture of ghee, honey, and sesame seeds for the homa, followed by a homa of curd-rice.

All the substances mentioned in this fundamental rite should be subjected to homa; for each, one should perform homa using all the mantras contained within the maṇḍala, and for each, one should recite its respective mantra while sprinkling the substance with scented water.

"Just as previously described for the rite of manifesting objects, one should likewise perform the recitation; looking at the object with one's own eyes while mentally reciting the mantra, by performing this ritual, the object is immediately consecrated through invocation. For all objects, by performing this rite of invocation, swift accomplishment is attained."

"In all the rites of offering and sacrifice belonging to this primary practice, one should perform each of these invitation rites in full; within the maṇḍala, one may also universally receive and maintain those objects, and one may also universally illuminate those objects.
If one performs the *sādhana* therein, those who create obstacles shall find no opportunity, and the objects will be universally purified.
Furthermore, according to the method of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), one may universally empower those objects and also universally empower oneself."
This is the secret and supreme maṇḍala capable of accomplishing all tasks; if one performs this rite, success will be attained before long.

Chapter Thirty-Six: On Supplementary Rites for Deficiencies. In the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Six, "On Supplementary Rites for Deficiencies," it is said: "I shall now explain the rites for supplementing deficiencies."
Having received and maintained the object, one should bathe three times daily;
perform offerings and homa three times a day while pressing the object with the hand;
change clothes three times a day; abstain from food on festival days; and all methods such as making offerings must be increased accordingly.
Perform prostrations, repentance, sympathetic joy, entreaty, and the making of vows during the three periods of the day;
recite scriptures and construct maṇḍalas during the three periods;
and take refuge and receive the precepts during the three periods.
By protecting the body during the three periods [of the day], one will certainly achieve accomplishment through the performance of this rite.
Alternatively, if any deficiency occurs due to negligence, one should recite the Mother-mantra of the Family twenty-one times, and it will then be made complete.

If this rite is omitted, the accomplishment will likewise be deficient; or, if there is any omission, one must further recite it one hundred thousand times and again construct this maṇḍala to compensate for the previous deficiency before proceeding with the accomplishment.
"In that maṇḍala, one should establish four gates at the four corners and arrange the boundary lines as previously described.
On the eastern side, place the Buddha;
on his right, place the Buddha’s ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure); and on his left, place the Buddha’s śalākā (dental probe)."
On the right side, place the Buddha Maitreya; on the left side, place the Buddha Locanā.
On the right side, place the Cakravartin-uṣṇīṣa; on the left side, place the Sitātapatrā-uṣṇīṣa.
On the right side, place Tejorāśi; on the left side, place the Vijaya-uṣṇīṣa.
Place the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-vijaya on the right side, Subhūti on the left side,
and Ānanda on the right side.
Place the almsbowl in the southwest corner.
Place the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) in the northwest corner.
Outside the gate, place Hārītī on the right side and Aparājitā on the left.
Outside the maṇḍala, place Sarvakarmakarī.
Place a wheel in the center;
upon it, place the object to be accomplished,
or alternatively, the principal deity.
"In the outer courtyard, place the deities of the eight directions;

on both sides of the gate, place the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda. Invite each with their respective root mantra, or invite them all together with the heart-mantra of the family (*kula-hṛdaya*). Offer worship according to the ritual rules, and then perform *homā* for these various deities, either by placing their mudrās or by placing their seats."
Having purified the fire with the root mantra, perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings of clarified butter and honey;

furthermore, perform one hundred *homa* offerings each of curd-rice and sesame seeds, using the root mantra for each. When these rites are completed, recite the mantra one hundred times again. This is the secret method for remedying transgressions.

"All items offered must be fragrant and delicious; the food presented for consumption should consist of *mūlaka* offerings mixed with granulated sugar and curd. For one who performs this rite, all the Honored Ones will be fully satisfied and delighted, and success shall be attained."

Not only to compensate for deficiencies, but also every half-month, on festival days, or even daily, one should construct this maṇḍala and make offerings to the various deities; thus all shall be nourished and fulfilled, and swift accomplishment will be attained.
If one cannot provide [the materials], one should act according to one's capacity.

"The ritual for the maṇḍala of the Buddha Family as previously described applies equally to this Lotus Family ritual; the only difference is that it is made circular, and its dimensions may be according to one's preference."
Place Avalokiteśvara in the center;
place Hayagrīva on the right side and Viśvarūpa on the left;
place Dvilocana on the right side and Caturbhuja on the left.
On the right side place the Six-Armed One; on the left side place the Twelve-Armed One.
On the right side place the Fulfiller of All Wishes;
furthermore, on the right side place Yaśodharā, and on the left side place Mahāśrī.
To the right, place Tārā; to the left, place Caṇḍa.
Near the door, to the right, place Śvetā; to the left, place Phaṇaravasinī. In the center, place a lotus.
Outside the maṇḍala, place the principal deities of the family who can accomplish all tasks; this is the Lotus Family’s method for supplementing deficiencies in the maṇḍala.
"As previously described for the Buddha Family maṇḍala, this Vajra Family [maṇḍala] is likewise; however, it must be made square, and its dimensions may be according to one's preference."
On the east side, place Vajrapāṇi;
on the right side, place the Vidyārāja, and on the left side, place Mañjughoṣa;
on the right side, place the wrathful Krodha-Śaṃkara, and on the left side, place Vajrāṅkuśa.
On the right side place Daṇḍa; on the left side place Mahābala.
On the right side place Muṣṭika; on the left side place Śumbha.
On the right side place Utkrośaka; on the left side place Pāṇini-kṣapa.
To the right, place the Wrathful Fire.
To the right, near the entrance, place Vajrabhairavanetra; to the right, near the entrance, place Aparājita-vajra.
Outside the maṇḍala, place the deities of the respective families who accomplish all tasks. All other matters concerning the outer precincts and the methods of offering are as previously described.
This is the rite for remedying deficiencies in the Vajra Family.

Having completed these offerings, one should seek auspicious dreams; then, at dawn, bathe and don clean white garments. Offer rice blossoms, green kuśa grass, and fragrant white flowers upon the ground where the maṇḍala is to be made, and thereafter smear it all over with cow dung and sweep it clean.
Perform the *tripātahoma* once more.
Place *kūśa* grass, fuel sticks, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey, sesame seeds, and rice on the right side.

All items for the *homa* are to be placed on the right; place the *argha* vessel, the ladle for the clarified butter, and the ladles for the various other substances on the left side, positioned directly in front.

Melted butter is placed next in front of the ladle; one sprinkles the objects and so forth with the Sarvakarmasādhaka mantra, invites the presiding deity of the family to be installed and offered to, and likewise installs the principal deity by inviting them with the *argha* using their respective root mantra.
Place ghee before oneself;
place fire before the ghee;
and place the object of accomplishment between the ghee and the fire.
First one's own body;
next, clarified butter;
next, material objects.
Next is fire;
next are the Principal Deity and the Lord of the Family.
One should know that the five aforementioned substances are to be placed in the following order.
"To the left of the Lord of the Family, place the Vidyā of Ajita; to the right, place Sarvakarmasādhaka.
Arrange them in the sequence as previously described in the homa ritual."

First, spread out blue *kubjaka* grass, place a mixture of rice and curd, scatter grains of rice, and present the offering of *svasti*. Make offerings with excellent and beautiful incense, and thereafter perform the homa rites according to the ritual rules.

"The accomplished object should be placed in a vessel made of gold, silver, refined copper, stone, conch, shell, wood, or *rāmi-kā* clay; having spread the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon it, place the vessel thereon;
or spread the leaves of a milky tree;
or the leaves of the *argha* tree."
One may spread out either leaves of a plantain tree, or leaves of a lotus,
or a fresh, clean white cotton cloth, whichever is available.
Furthermore, one should first spread five layers of leaves upon the ground and place the articles for accomplishment thereon;
then, one should cover those articles with another five layers of leaves,
or alternatively, one may use a parasol.
Whether it be various garments or miscellaneous items,
one should first understand the vessel in which they are contained, and then perform the *tripuṭa* rite with an undistracted mind.
Illuminating the object with the light of the mind and sprinkling it, one holds a ladle in the hand and slowly scoops up the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Placing it upon the object while reciting the root mantra, one pours it into the hearth immediately upon reaching the syllable *svā* (pronounced *sà*) and touches the object again upon uttering the syllable *hā* (pronounced *hà*), then returns to the vessel of clarified butter.
In this manner, as one comes and goes through these three locations, contact with objects must not be interrupted; this is called the *tripāda-homa* rite.
One should perform it one thousand or one hundred times, or according to whether the mantra is recited in its extensive or abbreviated form.

Alternatively, one may perform the rites from the upper and lower [positions] through the light and heavy [mantras], up to twenty-one homa offerings; this is called the general limit for the number of recitations.
During the *tripāṭha* [period], one should use the ladle to sprinkle the substances everywhere until they are all thoroughly moistened and saturated.
When first placing the objects, first sprinkle them with water, then press down upon them while reciting the mantra;
next, gaze at them with the eyes;
then present the offerings; once the homa is completed, one must again perform these steps in the same manner.

Regarding the three signs of accomplishment described for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala, if such signs appear while performing this rite, one must immediately observe the prohibitions; it should be known that accomplishment will be attained before long.
If the object is large, place it on the right side; if it is something to be held with the right hand, place it on the left side and perform the *triparyāsa* (three-fold tossing).
If the object is a sentient being, fashion its image and perform the *homa* while touching its head with the ladle;
if it is one's own person, perform the *homa* by touching the crown of one’s head with the ladle.
If one performs the *tripaṭa* rite for the sake of another, one should perform the *homā* while merely uttering that person's name.
Furthermore, there are three distinctions regarding the objects of accomplishment:
first, merely uttering the name;...
Second, one covers it with an object;
third, one merely exposes it so that it is visible to the eye.
In all such cases, one performs the homa using ghee.
If ghee is not obtained, one should use cow’s milk;
or use ghee mixed with milk;
or use the "three sweets."
Alternatively, one should employ curd according to the distinctions of the visualization of accomplishment;
or perform homa as originally described;
or perform homa with sesame oil for weapons.
If one is accomplishing a Vidyādhara, one should perform homa with the heartwood of a hard timber;
or use various resinous incenses such as *sugandha*;
or, observing the specific nature of the object and the particular nature of the accomplishment, one should take various types of fragrant substances that correspond to the rite and perform the homa.
If dog meat is used, its fat should likewise be employed; the same applies to all other types of meat.

As for the substances to be accomplished, they may either be placed entirely before [the practitioner] or offered according to the *sarpata* method as previously described, or by means of the *homa* ritual. One should extensively perform the *sarpata* method and the *homa* of those substances; having done so, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
"Having washed and rinsed the *tripatāka* until it is pure, one should then perform the consecration according to the ritual rules.

Once the consecration is complete, one should offer worship and maintain the object before the deity; furthermore, one should provide various kinds of food and drink as offerings to the deity and also perform sacrifices to the eight world-protectors of the directions. One must likewise properly perform the fire offering (*homa*) at the site of worship."

Thereafter, having bathed according to the proper ritual using various cleansing powders and *āmalaka* fruits, one should press the object with the hands at the hour of midday while performing recitation.

Furthermore, prepare a separate thread and recite the mantra over it according to the previous ritual method; likewise, for the armlet, water, ashes, and white mustard seed water, each must be consecrated with the recitation as performed previously.
"When one wishes to perform a rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), these articles for protecting the body must first be consecrated through recitation (*japa*) for later use.

When such articles for protecting the body have been accomplished through recitation, they will produce results immediately whenever they are employed; therefore, they must be consecrated in advance."
One must also prepare offerings such as flowers and, having performed the ritual recitation (*dhāraṇī-japa*), place them nearby.

Next, one should construct a maṇḍala according to the rite, perform the offerings, and carry out the *sādhanā*. Reciting the mantra capable of accomplishing all tasks, one should wrap the colored boundary lines around the four stakes; then, reciting the Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta (Muṇḍarī) mantra, one should place the ritual vases in front of the outer gate.
Tie both ends of the thread used for binding to the neck of the flask, leaving it slightly loose. Whenever entering or exiting, one should contemplate Mañjuśrī while holding the thread as one enters.
This thread may be consecrated by reciting the Mañjuśrī mantra, or it may be consecrated by reciting the mantra of the specific ritual method being employed.
Regarding the aforementioned methods for dispelling obstacles: first purify the site, and only then perform the ritual.
At that time, offer sacrifices outside to the great world-protecting deities of the eight directions along with their retinues;
place a *vajra* upon the ritual flask, or alternatively, place a branch bearing fruit.
One should protect that place by reciting the mantra of the vidyārāja of the respective family,
or using the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra) of the family,
or using the *kula-mātṛ* (family mother-mantra).
Alternatively, one may place the various mudrās belonging to their respective sections in their own directions to ward off all obstacles.

As for the stakes, one should recite the Vajrakilaya mantra one hundred times; the upper end of each stake should be fashioned in the shape of a three-pronged or a single-pronged vajra. Having done so, they are driven into the four corners outside the purified ritual chamber.
If one constructs a maṇḍala, one should drive it into the corners of the boundary lines; this is called the Vajra-Nail Method, which is capable of accomplishing all tasks.
That maṇḍala may be drawn using dry powdered colors, or various kinds of fragrant powders, or with wet pigments applied using a brush made of cow hair.
Outside each corner, draw a three-pronged vajra; throughout the boundary paths, fashion them all into the shape of three-pronged vajras, and recite the Vajraprākāra mantra over them.
Furthermore, within the shape of these boundary vajras, place another vajra laid horizontally; this should be done everywhere in this manner, which is then called the "Vajra Railing" (Vajravedikā).
Furthermore, one should recite the Vajrāṅkuśa mantra; having performed this, nothing shall be able to destroy it.
Therefore, one should perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*) therein. At each of the gates and outside the gates, one should place a vajra (*vajra*) respectively.

As for the method of accomplishment, it may be performed in a purified chamber or in the open air. The maṇḍala should measure five cubits, or seven, or eight; it should be made according to the scale of the matter to be accomplished, whether large or small.
"Place a vajra at each of the gates;
place vases upon each of the corners;
and place a vase for accomplishing all tasks in front of the outer gate."
"Place the Dharma-wheel mudrā on the inner eastern side;
place the Buddha-eye on the right side;
and place the Buddha-ūrṇā on the left side."
Place the *daṃṣṭrā-mudrā* on the right and the *śakti-mudrā* on the left;
place the five kinds of *uṣṇīṣas* on the right and left in successive order.
Within the Buddha Family (*buddha-kula*), all the honored deities should be placed on the left and right according to their sequence, with Ānanda and Subhūti positioned at the two final sides.
Next, place the Invincible One below near the gate.
Then, in the eastern side of the outer enclosure, place the Vidyārāja Siddhārtha;
in the northern side, place the Supreme Lord Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
On the south face, place the Honored One Mañjuśrī;
on the west face, place the Honored One Senāpati.
On the east face, place Brahmā and the various devas of the Form Realm on the right, and Indra on the left, extending upward from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven down to the terrestrial deities.
"In the southeast, place the Fire God with the various ṛṣis as his retinue;
in the south, place King Yama with the piśācas, bhūtas, and various mātṛs as his retinue;
in the southwest, place the deity Nairṛti with the various rākṣasas as his retinue."
To the south of the western gate, place the deity Varuṇa with the hosts of nāgas as his retinue;
to the north of the gate, place the Earth Deity with the asuras as his retinue;
in the northwest, place the Wind Deity with the garuḍas as his retinue.
In the north, place the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa with the yakṣas as his retinue;
in the northeast, place the deity Īśāna with the kumbhāṇḍas as his retinue.
Furthermore, in one location on the eastern side, place the Sun Deity (Sūrya) along with the planets;
and in one location on the western side, place the Moon Deity (Candra) surrounded by the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
On both sides of the bend at the western gate, place the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda.

Within the Buddha division, all the mantra-holders and vidyās belonging to the messengers and their like should be installed at will on the four sides of the outer courtyard; thereafter, according to the ritual, perform the invocation, followed by the sequence of offerings, homa, and recitation.

Place the principal deity or the object of accomplishment in the very center; just as the rites for protecting the body and so forth are described in the maṇḍala rituals, these should likewise be performed in this same sequence.
This is the Maṇḍala for Accomplishing All Objects belonging to the Buddha Family.
No obstacles whatsoever can find an opportunity there; by performing rites within it, one swiftly attains accomplishment, and all the Honored Ones increase their protective guardianship.
"As before, construct a maṇḍala using five colors, with the modification that it is square rather than circular.
Within its inner court, place the lotus seal at the center of the eastern side."
To the right, place the Seven Tārā Vidyās; to the left, place the Seven Auspicious Vidyās.
Next, place the Six Great Vidyārājñīs to the left and right;
to the right, place Pañcavaktrasiṃhī, and to the left, place Yaśomatī.
On both sides near the gate, place the One-Braided Vidyārājñī and Hayagrīva.
In front of the outer gate, place the *sarvakarmika-kalaśa* (vase that accomplishes all activities);
at the gates and corners, place vajras; and in the center, place a lotus.

In the outer enclosure, one should place Brahmā, Indra, Maheśvara, and other gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; as well as the Bodhisattvas Vimalacaryā, Prabhāmandita, and Alaṃkāra; and the Nāga Kings Ananta, Śuṇḍa, and Upaśuṇḍa; and the Vidyādhara King Śaṅkha together with all the other Vidyādharas, just like the World-Protectors of the various directions mentioned previously. Within this section, all types of messengers, mantras, and vidyās should be installed according to one’s preference. The sequence of installation is exactly as previously described, so that no obstacles whatsoever can find an opportunity; one should perform the rites of accomplishment within this [enclosure].
"As previously described for the path according to the boundary, place Susiddhikara on the eastern side of the inner courtyard;
to his right, place the Vidyārājñī Devaśrīvajra, and to his left, place the Vidyārājñī Vajramuṣṭi;
to the right, place the Vidyārāja Śumbha, and to the left, place the Vidyārāja Kīlikili."
To the right is placed the Vajra Honored One, and to the left is placed Vajradaṇḍa;
to the right is placed the Vajramudgara Hammer, and to the left is placed Vajraśaṅkara;
to the right is placed the Vajrāṅkuśī Consort, and to the left is placed the Māmakī Consort.
On the eastern side of the outer enclosure, place the messenger Vijñānaketu, the messenger Vajramati, Maheśvara and his consort, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, and the various yakṣas.
In front of the gate, one should prepare the various ritual vases.

Within the Vajra Family, all the mantras and vidyās of the messengers (dūtas), as well as the bhūtas, piśācas, gandharvas, mahoragas, vidyādharas, and the world-protectors of the eight directions, should each be installed in sequence in the outer enclosure. Thereafter, having invited them and made offerings according to the rite, one begins the accomplishment through fire-offerings (homa) and recitation.

Regarding the deities for whom one makes the invocation, one should use the mantras of the Vidyārājas or the mantras of the Kulasamayas; for each of the deities present in the maṇḍala, one should place a flask, just as one places flasks for all the rites of the aforementioned maṇḍala.
Just as all the dharmas of the aforementioned maṇḍalas, so too are all the methods for this accomplishment (*sādhana*).

"If one performs the accomplishment within these maṇḍalas, even if one does not fully possess the methods for protecting the body, one will still attain *siddhi*. This is because those deities themselves have made this vow:
'If anyone invites us to attend their maṇḍala and makes offerings according to the ritual with a sincere heart, we shall grant them whatever they seek.'"
Therefore, one should know that in this regard there will be no obstacles and protection will certainly be granted.

If one employs the Family Heart-mantra (*kulahṛdaya*), the Family Mother (*kula-mātṛ*), or the Vidyā Consort (*vidyārājñī*), as well as the mantras capable of accomplishing all tasks and the mantra for internal self-protection (*adhyātmarakṣā*) to perform the invocation, the various realms of self-protection will swiftly attain accomplishment.
This is the secret dharma of the three families.
Furthermore, the common secret maṇḍala of the three families shall now be explained.

As in the Path of the Dharmadhātu, one places a vajra; in the center, one places the seal (mudrā) of the presiding deity of the family; in front of that, one places the presiding mantra-deity. Alternatively, as previously described, one places a *kalaśa* vessel, filling it with substances such as those contained within a bowl or similar vessel, and sets it upon the [vajra].
"In the eastern side of the inner court, place the seal of the Tathāgata;
in the northern side, place the seal of Avalokiteśvara;
and in the southern side, place the seal of Vajra."
On the right side of the western face, place Rudra; on the left side, place the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
Just as in the previously explained Maṇḍala of the Vidyārājas, these should likewise be installed in this sequence.
On the right place the Vidyā of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ), and on the left place the Vidyā for Accomplishing Activities (Karmasādhanī).
It is the same for the two families of Padma and Vajra on the left and right.
On the western side, place Kṣāri on the right and Rakṣami on the left.
"Place the alms bowl and the *cīvara* at the two corners of the eastern side;
place the *daṇḍa* staff and the *kuṇḍikā* water flask at the two corners of the northern side;
and place the *vajra* and the *mudgara* hammer at the two corners of the southern side."
Place the *śūla* and the precious vase at the two corners on the western side.
At the outer gate, establish a separate location and place Aparājitā there.
Place Hārītī mother in front of the eastern gate.
Place Kuṭa-jihrika before the southern gate and Eka-citta before the northern gate.
In the outer enclosure, arrange the various mudrās as you wish;
invoke and make offerings according to the ritual rules. This is the secret universal maṇḍala; whatever substances are prepared for accomplishment within it will all attain siddhi.
Even Māra, who moves through the zenith, cannot find an opportunity here, let alone other *vināyakas*.

One should offer various fragrant incenses, flowers, lamps, and diverse foods while reciting with radiant clarity; the methods of offering as explained for the recitation and the maṇḍala should be performed in this same manner, and it is likewise to be done within a purified chamber.
The various offerings for the Lord of the Maṇḍala should be increased fourfold; this is the secret method.

Having completed the offerings, one should next perform the ritual sacrifice outside according to the rules, lighting lamps with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with fresh and pure wicks to worship the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Each and every item must be presented as an *argha* offering; if one performs the rite in this manner, swift efficacy will be attained.
Recite the mantra of the Vidyārāja over white mustard seeds, or use the mantra capable of accomplishing all tasks;

alternatively, use a mantra for which you have previously attained mastery through recitation. Place these near the object of accomplishment to ward off all obstacles, which will then immediately disperse.

Furthermore, place the mudrā of the lord of the respective family on the left side, or simply recite the mantra; place a great sword on the left side, and station a man at each of the eight directions.
First, in the east, that person assumes the attire of Śakra, holding a *vajra* in hand, with form and color exactly like Śakra;
in the south, that person assumes the attire of Yama, holding a *daṇḍa* staff in hand;
in the west, that person assumes the attire of a Nāga King, holding a noose (*pāśa*) in hand.
In the north, that person is dressed in the attire of Vaiśravaṇa, holding a *gadā* club in his hand;
in the northeast, that person is dressed in the attire of Īśāna, holding a three-pronged trident;
in the southeast, that person is dressed in the attire of the Fire God (*Agni*), appearing like a *ṛṣi*, holding a water jar (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣamālā*).
In the southwest, that person is dressed in the attire of a rākṣasa king, holding a horizontal sword in hand;
in the northwest, that person is dressed in the attire of a wind deity, holding a bannered flag in hand.

“Śakra is white; Yama is black; the Nāga King is red; Vaiśravaṇa is golden; Īśāna is white with a yellow tint; the Fire God is the color of fire; the Rākṣasa King is the color of a pale black cloud; and the Wind God is blue. The garments they wear are all likewise.”

All those persons must receive the precepts and ensure they are utterly pure; they must possess great courage and bravery, be skilled in the methods for protecting the body, have upright features, be in the prime of youth, and be robust and strong. All the weapons they carry must be consecrated through recitation, and they must wear flower garlands interlaced around their necks and both shoulders.
Prepare white mustard seeds; they are effective against obstacles and signs of adversity.
If an obstacle arrives, immediately scatter white mustard seeds and strike it with them, or throw a flower garland;
or, if the obstacles are numerous and manifest great terror, one should brandish the weapons one holds at them from a distance.

If they should press him closely and strike with weapons, he should scatter white mustard seeds and throw flower garlands while brandishing his own weapon; at the time of being struck, he must not move from his original position. If he moves from his original position, the opponent will gain the advantage; therefore, he must remain motionless in his place.
"Regarding all the invincible body-protection mudrās contained within this treasury, one should recite over them, make offerings to them, and keep them by one's side.

If a great and violent danger should arise, one should use those very mudrās to strike it away; or else, one may take white mustard seeds and strike the danger with them while reciting mantras that have been previously empowered through recitation."
If they still do not cease, one should go outside and perform a ritual sacrifice according to the Dharma, offering abundant and excellent food and drink to those various obstructing spirits.
There are nine kinds of general protections for the Dharma, namely:

expelling obstacles, binding the boundary of the earth, binding the boundary of space, binding the boundary of the maṇḍala, binding the directions and locations, binding the vajra wall, and binding the vajra railing to protect objects and the body, thereby removing all obstacles.
When performing the rite of accomplishment, one must keep such dharmas as these in mind.
"Alternatively, if one cannot provide the protective weapons for the respective directions, one should place the appropriate directional weapon there;
if even this is not available, one should place *nārāca* weapons in all the directions."
Alternatively, one may draw a bow and take up arrows, placing them in various locations;

or one may employ an assistant for the accomplishment who understands the *piṭaka* teachings, possesses wisdom and skillful means, has merit from recitation, and maintains pure conduct. Such a person should stand at the gate to assist in performing various tasks and ward off all obstacles, providing aid throughout both the inner and outer courtyards.
"All matters whatsoever must be fully prepared by evening. As soon as the sun has set, one should begin the accomplishment.
If one becomes weary during the process, one should go outside the maṇḍala, take water in the mouth to rinse, and drink three handfuls of water consecrated with the mantra of Kuṇḍalī;
or alternatively, one may drink a small amount of ghee consecrated with the heart-mantra of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā). By doing so, all exhaustion shall be cured."

Furthermore, mix long pepper with honey and, while reciting the vidyā-mantra of the Mother of the Buddha Family, apply it to the eyes; thus, even a state of mental dullness that is difficult to overcome will be immediately cured.

First, standing facing east with a sincere heart, observe the various deities, take refuge in them, and offer supplications. Among the three kinds of auspicious and fortunate signs, obtain whichever favorable sign you prefer, and perform the accomplishment (*sādhana*) with a joyful mind; as the initial omen was perceived, so too shall the accomplishment be.

Therefore, the practitioner should observe the preliminary omens; first, they must briefly contemplate the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara, and next, circumambulate it clockwise while preparing the vessel for all rites.

When entering the maṇḍala, one should circumambulate all the vases encountered, keeping them to the right. Having arrived, one prostrates to the deities and surveys them thoroughly, offering arghya with each deity’s respective root mantra, or otherwise making offerings to those invoked with the heart-mantra of their family.
"O Lords of Mantras, you should summon [the deities] with the mantras of the Vidyārājas;
and the Vidyārājas thus summoned should be summoned by means of the Vidyārājñīs.

Having summoned them, each should display their respective original mudrās and recite their original mantras and vidyās, or alternatively, simply display one universal mudrā and recite its mantra and vidyā. If one acts in this manner, one will swiftly attain siddhi."
"As for the accomplishment of the object, it may be placed within an *argha* vessel, or upon a flask;
or it may be held within cupped hands;
or it may be accomplished through mere mental recollection."
Alternatively, one may place them in *varmika* vessels;
or, having placed them upon leaves, one presses them inside.
All the vessels prepared before the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) should be smeared with ox-gallstone (*gorocanā*).
Next, use white mustard seeds to perform the protection;
next, recite the mantra while making offerings of mālatī flowers to the object.
By smearing it with ox-gall (gaurika), the object becomes secured through the rite of binding.
Using the mustard seeds constitutes the protection;
offering the flowers constitutes the illumination.
These three methods should be performed in their proper sequence and must not be omitted or neglected.
"Place the articles for accomplishment before the deity, ensuring that no other objects intervene between them.
These articles for accomplishment are protected by two methods:
first, by means of mudrās;"
2. White mustard seeds:

because they cause the object of accomplishment to manifest results swiftly, one should repeatedly offer *argha*, flowers, incense, and other requisites, as well as curd. One should also frequently make offerings to those who assist in the accomplishment, so that they may protect the object and remain constantly at that place.

"Having thus arranged and made offerings, one should then press [the object] with the hand or gaze upon it with the eyes, reciting the mantra slowly with an undistracted mind, repeatedly manifesting its splendor throughout the process."

In this manner, one should continue the recitation throughout the entire night without interruption. During the three periods of that night, one should perform offerings in succession with *argha* water and other substances.
If it becomes necessary to go outside to rinse the mouth, one should have an assistant take one’s place before the ritual objects and continue the recitation;
whatever portion of the recitation the practitioner has omitted, the assistant must compensate for and complete.
If a great calamity should arise while performing the recitation, those assisting in its accomplishment should repel that calamity.
If they are unable to restrain it, the practitioner should personally scatter white mustard seeds to ward off the disaster.
"When a person who assists in the practice recites this object, if such difficulties as heavy rain and lightning appear in the east at that time, one should know them to be the obstacles of Śakra."
In the southeast, this obstacle appears: a great being of fiery color, or like the midday sun; one should know this to be the obstacle of the Fire God (Agni).

In the south, this obstacle appears: a corpse of most terrifying form, crying out with a loud voice, holding a great sword, having all its noses cut off, holding a skull filled with human blood, with fire burning upon its head; one should know this to be the obstacle of Yama.
In the southwest direction, this obstacle manifests, namely the raining down of excrement.
The filth of excrement covers the maṇḍala in various forms that are most terrifying; one should know that this is precisely the obstacle of Nīlāṭi.
In the western direction, there are these manifest calamities, namely rain, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, hail, and so forth; one should know that these are the calamities of the dragon kings.
In the northwest, this difficulty appears, namely:
a great black wind arises; one should know that this is the difficulty caused by the Wind Deity.
In the north, this difficulty appears, namely: great yakṣas and female yakṣas disturb the practitioner; one should know that this is the difficulty caused by the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

In the northeast, such obstacles appear: those with the heads of elephants, pigs, and dogs, each with a different form and holding a great mountain; one should know that these are the obstacles of Īśāna.
One should know that when various devas manifest above with great majestic power, this is the calamity of the upper heavens.
When the earth below shakes and cracks, one should know this is the calamity of the asuras.

"When the highest accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*) is being performed, these obstacles appear; such obstacles manifest during the middle watch of the night. One should know that for ordinary [accomplishments], the signs of obstacles in the highest accomplishment are likewise great, while those for middling and lower accomplishments should be understood accordingly."

During the three periods of the night, if these signs—superior, middling, and inferior—correspond with the proper time, it is accomplishment; if they do not correspond with the time, it is not accomplishment.
"As for those three signs, they are warmth, smoke, and light; these three signs should appear in successive order."
If the superior accomplishment is achieved, one possesses all three characteristics;
if the middling accomplishment is achieved, one possesses the first two characteristics;
if the inferior accomplishment is achieved, only the first characteristic is manifested.

Alternatively, if while reciting with devotion the three signs appear in succession during the first watch of the night, one should immediately restrain their radiance by means of the Family Mother mantra;
or restrain those signs by means of the Heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja;
and furthermore, apply and sprinkle powdered ox-gall while reciting.
Some press with their hands;
some sprinkle with clarified butter;
or some scatter flowers.
Alternatively, one may use white mustard seeds;
or, by merely sprinkling water and performing the rite of "prohibiting" (nirodha) the signs, one may immediately enjoy [the substance] and likewise fulfill the vow.

Or, if it is accomplished during the first watch of the night, one should perform the rite of "prohibiting" and recitation, and only at the designated time may one enjoy it. One should understand that the accomplishment within this interval follows this same principle.
"In the first watch of the night, the lower siddhi is accomplished;
in the middle watch of the night, the middling accomplishment is obtained;
when the dawn light appears, the supreme accomplishment is obtained."

Among these, for one who has achieved the middling accomplishment, once they have performed the ritual prohibitions according to the Dharma, they may utilize [the substances] even until dawn; the lower accomplishments should be understood accordingly.

Regarding those things that are accomplished at their respective times, it is not auspicious even if they are not utilized; for even if the object is accomplished, if it is not used immediately and is not preserved, and one does not utilize the object by dawn, it will be like a withered flower or foul food, unfit for use. Because the mantra was invoked through recitation to enter into the object, once the time has passed, its efficacy is lost.

Furthermore, although the signs of accomplishment may initially appear, they do not yet constitute actual accomplishment; however, if at that time one restrains those signs and subsequently performs rites such as the manifestation of light, as well as offerings and consecrations on festival days, then accomplishment is achieved.
If, after three years, it is not accomplished, one should know that this object cannot be perfected.
For the supreme accomplishment, the limit is three years;
for the middling accomplishment, it is six months.
If the lower grade of accomplishment is not restricted by time, the method for accomplishing auspicious signs is likewise so.
Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Method for Recovering Stolen Accomplished Objects from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "I shall now explain the method for recovering objects that have been stolen."
When the object has been completed, or at the time of performing the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the object may be stolen;
either its form is seen at the moment of theft, or the object is simply lost without the thief being seen.
At that time, one need not select an auspicious day or observe a fast; rather, when anger arises before one, this maṇḍala rite should be performed immediately.

Construct it using triangular funeral ashes, opening only the western gate. Place the principal deity (bimba) at the outer gate, and place the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara in the eastern corner of the inner court.
To the right, place Vajracanda; to the left, place Mahācanda.
To the right, place Vajramuṣṭi; to the left, place Vajrāṅkuśa.
To the right, place Vajrakīlikīla; to the left, place Vemacitra.
Place Raudra on the right and Bhṛṅgiriṭi on the left;
place Aśani on the right and Śaṃkara on the left;
place Vīryamukha on the right and Kārimukha on the left.
To the left, place Durdharṣa and Vajrasena;
to the right, place Sumbha and the other great wrathful deities.
For the sake of accomplishment, arrange them in their proper order and invoke them according to the ritual rules, making successive offerings of red flowers, red food, and so forth.

"The *ābhicāruka* rites previously described should be performed here; the principal deity stationed outside the gate should be worshipped according to the ritual with exquisite flowers and other offerings.
Furthermore, the deities of the eight directions and the various other messengers (*dūta*) of the respective families stationed in the outer enclosure must likewise be worshipped in this manner."
"In its center, perform the homa rite; the hearth shall be triangular, exactly as described before. Use seven *kṣudradīrā* stalks, anoint them with one's own blood, and perform the homa;
or use *kaṭuka* wood, or the remains of firewood used for cremating a corpse to perform the homa.
Once the fire has been kindled, mix the ashes from the cremation with one's own blood and perform the homa."
Furthermore, one should perform *homa* by mixing four substances—poison, one’s own blood, mustard oil, and red mustard seeds—and using them together.

Then, taking these same four substances, one fashions the form of a thief, sits upon it, and with the left hand, cuts it into pieces and performs *homa*. This rite should be performed by those who have subdued their anger and those who are proficient in the methods of the gate.
When the thief, seized by panic and terror, brings the stolen object and personally offers it, the practitioner should grant him fearlessness and perform the *śāntika* rite for him at that time;
if this is not done, he will die, or else the object he brought shall increase in value and be secretly placed before the Honored One.

Furthermore, if one has stolen an object and many days have passed, and one wishes to recover it, one should perform this rite using the *Sarvakarmasādhana-maṇḍala* common to the three families, constructed as a square with the seal of the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara installed at its center.

"On the southern side of the inner court, one should place Vajrakrodha, Mahākrodha, Māmakī, Vajrāṅkuśa, Bhojana, Vajramuṣṭi, Vajrajvālā, Vajramātṛ, Tekara, Vajrabhairava, Vajraśaṅkaraloha, Kīlikīla, Prajñāvajra, Aparājita, as well as all the great wrathful deities, all the messengers (dūtas), and the lords of mantras of great majesty; these should be arranged in sequence on its southern side."

"On the northern side of the inner court are placed the Avalokiteśvara Who Fulfills All Wishes, Hayagrīva, the many-faced and many-armed Yaśomatī who can manifest in many forms, Mahāśrī, Rakṣami, Śvetā, Pañcaravasinī, Tara, Candra, and Māra."
All mantras and vidyās, as well as the various messengers, are each to be installed in their respective order according to the ritual rules.

On the eastern side of the inner enclosure, one places the *Suvarṇacakravarti-uṣṇīṣa* and other such uṣṇīṣas, as well as the Buddha-ūrṇā, Buddha-netrī, Buddha-śakti, Buddha-danta, Buddha-maitrī, Aparājita, and other lords of vidyās, along with all other mantras capable of accomplishing tasks and all other messengers; these are each to be installed on the eastern side in their respective order according to the ritual rules.
Those positioned on both sides near the gate and outside the gate are likewise to be installed according to the ritual procedures as described before.
Regarding the deities of the eight directions in the outer enclosure: place Brahmā and his retinue on the southern side of the western gate;
place Maheśvara together with his consort, Yanapatti, and their various attendants on the northern side of the western gate.
Furthermore, the seven Mātṛkās, the eight Nāga Kings along with their retinues,
and the Asura Kings with their retinues—

all those deities of great majesty who have taken refuge in the Buddha— are each to be installed in due order according to the ritual rules within the outer enclosure; they are to be invoked with utmost sincerity and offered worship in succession.

"To the west outside, place a homa fire pit. Fashion an effigy of the thief out of wax and place it within a winnowing basket; then, according to the ābhicāruka rite, perform the invocation, sacrifice, offerings, and homa.
Next, cut the effigy with a knife and perform the homa."
Alternatively, one may perform it according to the *abhicāru* rites taught in one’s own family (*kula*);
or one may perform it in the same manner when the deity steals [the substance] itself, or when it is accomplished even though it was not given.
From the fifth day to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, performing the ritual during this interval is said to lead to supreme attainment.

Furthermore, one may strike his form with a staff or whip, scorch it with fire, or beat it with various fierce implements; one may pierce his body with a *mudgara* (pestle) or a *vajrakīla* (vajra-stake);
or one may smear his entire body with black mustard seeds, oil, and salt, inflicting harm upon him according to one’s will through such agonizing tortures.
Furthermore, cover the form with a shroud used for a corpse;

wrap it with red thread, offer red flowers, and while reciting the mantra, stare at it with eyes wide open. Insert words of censure into the mantra and strike it every day; if anyone brings an object [to you], you should then cease.
"In the middle watch of the night, one should perform this fierce rite: using *kubjaka* wood smeared with black mustard oil, one should perform *homa*;
furthermore, mixing poison, one's own blood, mustard seeds, oil, salt, and black mustard seeds together, one should perform *homa* eight hundred times while reciting the name of the thief;
or alternatively, one may simply mix one's own blood with salt and perform *homa*."
If, after such disciplinary measures have been applied, the object is not returned, one must employ even more severe methods until death.
One should perform all the rites for killing as described in the *Abhicāruka* (sorcery) section, and insert the words of killing into the mantra.
If someone brings an object and requests that the practice be ceased, one should grant them joy.
If they have already used the object and bring another to replace it, one should likewise cease the matter.
Or, if they have already used the object and have nothing to replace it, yet come to offer an apology and express regret, one should also cease the matter and bestow joy upon them.
If he should suffer a loss or give it away to another, then regarding whatever remains that is brought back, one should cease the matter and bestow joy upon him.
One should perform homa with the Vajra-cenara mantra;
or perform homa with Mahā-krodha, or with Aśuci-krodha.
Alternatively, one may perform *homa* using the mantras for recovering lost items taught in the respective section.
However, these three types of mantras are applicable across all three families.
The mantra is as follows: "Namaḥ..."
Ratnatrayāyaṃ mañjuśrīkrodha.
Vajrapāṇaye maṅgalya-kṣaṇāṃ pratīccha oṃ.
Hara hara vajra.
Manta Manta Svavajra (Manta Manta [Sva]vajra)
Dhana-dhana va-jra.
Hana hana vajra-pātra.
Pātra is vajranara.
Naravajranara-yaḥ (Naravajranāraya)
Naraya-vajra naraya.
Vināyavajracchinda!
HĀ HŪṂ VAJRA PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. Wrath Depart!
Vajra Phaṭ! Svāhā!
Bhṛkuṭī vajra hūṃ.
"Phaṭ. Once the object has been obtained, or a substitute has been obtained, one should immediately protect that object as well as oneself.
On the auspicious days, one should perform the rites of illumination and so forth in their proper sequence.
Among these, one portion of the accomplished substances and the minor accomplishments should be offered to the World-Honored One;
one portion should be offered to the ācārya;
and having gone outside the maṇḍala, one should take another portion and offer it to those who have previously attained accomplishment.
One portion should be given to companions and others;
take the fifth portion for one's own use, or divide it into two parts—one for personal use and one to be offered to the four places.
All things that have not yet been acquired are likewise treated in this manner.

First, one offers *argha* water to the Honored Ones and others, and afterwards takes one's own portion. As for the portion belonging to those who have previously attained accomplishment, one honors them with *argha* and takes it for one's own use by paying its price; here, "price" refers to the offering itself.

If the ācārya is absent, one may take possession of that share after compensating it with its value; as for those who feel shame regarding the value, their sense of moral remorse constitutes the payment of that value.
"When performing the rite for honoring the predecessors outside the maṇḍala, one should speak these words:
'May all those who have previously attained accomplishment accept their respective portions.
Holding the argha vessel in hand, one should chant thus a second and a third time:"
"If there is no one to take it, you should immediately give it to your companions; do not harbor any doubt.

Because they possess a devout mind, because they have made offerings, because they maintain the precepts, and because they have served as attendants, they are those who have already attained realization; therefore, they should receive their share."
When the third proclamation is made, those companions should respond thus:
"We are indeed those who have previously attained accomplishment.
The practitioner shall then divide the objects among his companions.
"If the substance is so small that it cannot be divided—such as agallochum, cow bezoar, and the like, which are indivisible—one should mentally determine its portion and use it for oneself."

There are such items that are for the use of a single person alone and cannot be divided, such as wheels, swords, and the like; one should perform the accomplishment according to what is taught in the specific root text, and the same applies to painted scrolls and images, which likewise cannot be divided.

Regarding the substances for accomplishment within this root practice, even if their quantity is small, one may add to the original amount to perform the accomplishment so that it is equal to that of the companions;
or, one may perform the accomplishment based on the size of a person already accomplished, and even if it is reduced by half, accomplishment is still attained;
or, one must act according to the specific proportions prescribed in the root practice.
"When a traveler distributes goods to his companions, he should instruct them, saying:
'You shall follow my various commands.
Only after they have given their assent should he give them [the goods]."

Whether it be a single individual accomplishing the benefit of others, or the distribution of property among companions and associates, it is universally permitted within this scriptural treasury or other teachings that such matters should be settled according to the limits of each person's labor;
one must not be partial or biased in the apportionment of goods.

Once the substance has been accomplished, one should first make offerings to the principal deity; having generated deep shame and remorse and having made earnest requests again, one may then distribute it. This applies to all the rituals of every *kula*.

The middling and lower grades of accomplishment should be understood according to this principle: one should give rise to deep shame and remorse, offer respectful service and worship, and bestow material wealth; furthermore, one should comply with the instructions regarding all movements and conduct, repaying the price of the object through such actions.

Once the substance has been accomplished, first offer *argha* water; then, according to the ritual, distribute it while reciting the root mantra and performing the hand gestures (*mudrā*). Contemplate the principal deity with the mind and recite the mantra of the Queen of Wisdom until the visualization is complete. Thereafter, one may enjoy the substance. At will, one ascends into the sky and arrives at the abode of the sages; there, no one can harm or despise them, and even if there are enemies, they cannot cause any injury.

"The practitioner who has attained accomplishment must constantly keep the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) in mind and never forget them. The articles of accomplishment must always be kept in mind or observed with the eyes. Because one recites the mantras of the Vidyārāja, all the ṛṣis will pay him homage; because one holds the consort's mantra, there shall be no fear. One must not neglect performing the samaya-mudrā and the family (kula) mudrā, nor the observation of objects with the eyes."
Upon meeting a seer, one should first show respect and inquire, saying:
"Welcome; are you at ease? From where have you come?
One should then answer whatever he may ask with well-spoken words.
"When traveling through the air, one should not pass over shrines, solitary trees, crossroads, the dwellings of sages, cities, sacrificial altars, or places where Brahmins assemble."
If one passes beyond the abode of the hosts of heretical ṛṣis due to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), one will surely fall upon passing through them.
For those who fall due to negligence, they should recite the mantras of the Vidyārāja and engage in contemplation;

whether they have already fallen or are on the verge of falling, they shall regain their original station in space. Although it is devoid of form or color, it is a path seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); just as a practitioner reaches his destination as soon as he forms the intention, or as one who remains in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) arrives without moving.

"Therefore, one travels upon that path previously perfected; by the power of merit, garments appear spontaneously according to one's wish. There are palaces, flowers, groves, gardens, and various birds; celestial maidens roam about offering songs, dances, and music. All manner of sensual pleasures blaze with radiant light, and the wish-fulfilling kalpa-tree can satisfy all desires."

For their dwelling, they have seats made of precious gems; beneath flowing channels, soft grasses are spread upon the ground. There are various necklaces and ornaments for adorning the body, as well as objects of entertainment. Auspicious trees bear fruits of ambrosia, and even whatever places one desires or recalls appear before them.

Even though this is so, one must always protect the body and not neglect it; one should dwell in pure groves, on mountain peaks, or on islands in the sea, at riverbanks and sandbars, staying in those places for the sake of recreation. There, one will encounter the superior environments described previously, or dwell together with the assembly of sages who have already attained perfection.
Furthermore, as previously explained, one should perform the rites for *siddhi* with full completeness.

Should the object not be accomplished, one should restrain it according to the ritual, guard it, and set it aside; then, as before, one should again perform the preliminary recitation methods, proceeding even to the rites for accomplishment once more.
If, after acting in this way, it is still not accomplished, one should increase one's diligence and again perform the recitation and the rites for accomplishment.
If, after reciting the sūtra in this manner for seven full cycles, success is still not achieved, one should perform this rite for certain accomplishment.
That is to say:
beg for alms, practice with diligent recitation, arouse great reverence, circumambulate the eight holy sites, and prostrate while walking the path.
Alternatively, one may recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seven times or one hundred times;
or offer superior objects as gifts to the Saṃgha;
or [recite it] by the banks of rivers that flow into the sea;

Alternatively, on a sea island, one should construct one hundred *stūpas*, each measuring one cubit (*hasta*). Before each *stūpa*, one should perform the recitation according to the ritual until it is completed one thousand times. If, at the end, the hundredth *stūpa* emits light, one should know that the rite has been definitively accomplished.

"If one subsequently constructs one thousand stūpas and recites [the mantra] one thousand times before each one, even if the number of *ānantarya* sins has been reached, they will be naturally purified without the need for further ritual procedures;
furthermore, if one recites any mantra one *koṭi* times, it will certainly be accomplished.
If one recites while performing the rite for twelve years, even those with grave offenses will achieve accomplishment, and even if the ritual requirements are incomplete, all will be accomplished."
Furthermore, once the recitation count and the time have been completed, one should immediately perform the *vṛddhi-homa* (prosperity rite);
or else, one may construct this Maṇḍala for Accomplishing All Aims (*sarvakarmasādhana*) and perform the four types of *homa* therein.
Either on a mountain peak,
or at a place where a herd of cattle previously resided,
or on an island in the Ganges— one should level the ground and construct a maṇḍala measuring one hundred and eight cubits, and place one hundred and eight jars within it.

At its four gates, pillars were erected to form the entrances; before each gate, jeweled terraces were established and adorned in various ways. Garlands made of branches of famous flowers were tied to the gate pillars and the corner banners, encircling the entire site.
One hundred and eight lamps fueled by ghee were arranged upon the maṇḍala, and one hundred and eight incense burners containing various renowned incenses were also placed there.
One side of the inner court measures seven cubits, one side of the outer court measures three cubits, and the remainder is the center.
All invocations, offerings, and so forth are exactly as before; following the homa ritual, they shall now be explained separately.
Within that space, place the *kalaśa* flask with the root mantra; perform the homa rite at the four sides of the flask.
On the eastern side of the inner courtyard, install all the deities of the Buddha Family;
on its northern side, install all the deities within the Lotus Family.
On its southern face, place all the deities belonging to the Vajra family;
on the western face, place the god Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa, each together with their respective retinues.
As previously described, the messengers and other honored deities should be placed in the outer court if they cannot be accommodated within the inner court.
The guardians of the directions and their respective retinues should each be placed in their own original positions;
the lords of the three families, as well as Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa, should first be placed in their original locations.
Next, one should further place the Vidyārājas, Vidyārājñīs, and the lords of mantras who accomplish activities, along with their respective messengers, arranging them in successive order;
and in front of the outer gate, one should place the Honored One Khaṇḍarohā and the Honored One Aparājita.
Having thus completed the mandala according to the ritual, one should perform the sequence of invocation and offerings using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of the respective family (*kula*).

Then, while performing recitation (*japa*) in the four directions, one should subsequently perform the homa rite within the hearths placed on the four sides of the flask, each according to its own family; this is called the "homa for the enhancement of the deities."
For the food offerings, present *uṇḍara*.
Having performed this, all the honored ones will become augmented.
"Having thus completed the recitation and the homa, further perform the homa of clarified butter with the mantra of the Family Mother."
Next, perform homa with milk porridge mixed with ghee using the mantra of the principal deity;
further, perform homa with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets using the mantra of the Family Mother (Kuleśvarī);
and again, perform homa with ghee using the mantra of the Family Mother.

Once this rite has been performed, all the Honored Ones will be fully satisfied; they will attain increase, perfection, and complete fulfillment, and with universal joy, they will swiftly grant accomplishment.
If one constructs this maṇḍala up to seven times, success will certainly be achieved.

If, despite performing the recitation and circumambulating the stūpa as previously described up to seven times while constructing this maṇḍala, success is not attained, one should then subdue the deity through the methods of *abhicāruka* (wrathful rites).
Fashion an image of the deity out of wax and recite its mantra. First, recite the mantras of the Family Mothers (*kula-mātṛ*) and the Vidyārājas;

place the mantra of the principal deity (*mūla-devatā*) in between. Perform a *homa* sacrifice according to the *ābhicāruka* rite, using mustard oil to smear the image, whereby it will suffer from a violent fever. If one intends to subjugate another, the entire body [of the victim] shall ache. Strike the image with a whip or flowers while maintaining a wrathful mind, making offerings with the aforementioned two mantras. Just as one punishes a malevolent spirit, the method for punishing the principal deity is likewise.

"Such a rite must be performed according to the instructions and not according to one's own arbitrary will; immediately upon doing so, the Honored One will appear before you and grant you accomplishment. Once your original vow is fulfilled, cease that previous activity and perform the śāntika rite."
Alternatively, having thoroughly mixed poison, one’s own blood, sesame seeds, oil, salt, and red mustard seeds together, perform homa throughout the entire night.
At that time, the tutelary deity will cry out in terror:
"Stop! Stop! Do not! Do not!"
"Grant me the accomplishment.

If, after performing this rite for three days, [the deity] still does not come to grant the accomplishment, one should again apply oneself with even greater vigor and, with a fearless mind, cut off one's own flesh and perform the homa three times. Then the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) will immediately appear; having been pleased by this, the deity will grant whatever boon is sought in one's heart.

If there are any deficiencies or transgressions, they shall be explained one by one; even if one has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, by performing the homa of flesh for nine nights, [the deity] will certainly come and grant accomplishment.
This is the method for contending with mantras; one must perform it only after protecting oneself according to the Dharma with a fearless mind, for it will certainly not be in vain.
Once success has been attained, one should immediately perform the śāntika rite.
If any faults or transgressions are mentioned, they must immediately be rectified; among all rites of accomplishment (*sādhana*), this maṇḍala is supreme.
Within it, by performing three types of activities, one obtains three types of fruits; therein, one should perform all manner of rites as well as *homa* offerings.

One should subdue the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) as one would subdue a malevolent spirit; for every ritual offering, one must use fresh materials, and the same applies to the items used for the *homa*.

This rite must not be undertaken with negligence; one should bathe until pure, protect the body according to the Dharma, and never treat it with contempt. Only one who clearly understands the scriptural teachings (*pitaka*) may employ this method to subdue the *iṣṭadevatā*; should one act contrary to this, one will surely bring harm upon oneself.

Regarding the *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Volume Lower: The national edition (Guoben) is identical to the Song edition, whereas the Dan edition alone differs. Having examined it, I found no authoritative basis for either version; thus, I have dared neither to omit nor to adopt, but have preserved both for the sake of future scholars and sages. This, then, is the Dan edition.
